#7812. LMLineage: Content Lineage and Context Governance for LLM Agents

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (251 w)

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

LMLineage: Content Lineage and Context Governance for LLM Agents

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (251 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.22511v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Interpretability for AI agents should not be confined to understanding the model's internal weights. It must also cover the agent's reasoning and decision-making process over multi-source context. We present LMLineage, an out-of-band system that attributes every output sentence of an agent session to its supporting input spans with calibrated confidences, without requiring white-box access to the model or any additional inference passes. On top of the lineage metadata, we build concept-drift micro compaction: instead of waiting for the context-length limit and summarizing everything, the system detects when previously used input documents have stopped being referenced ("drifted") and surgically compacts only those, preserving user instructions verbatim. We evaluate on a multi-tier corpus: 71 gold annotated sentences from 10 Chinese web-QA cases, plus 90 turns of independently collected multi-turn sessions across three generator models (gpt-4o-mini, qwen3.8-27b, deepseek-v4-flash). Results show that (i) window-level embedding similarity is far better aligned with LLM paraphrasing than whole document or lexical matching; (ii) the greedy-window fast path is both faster and more accurate on average than exhaustive line-matching (a multiple-comparisons bias in the latter inflates web recall at the cost of overall accuracy); (iii) per-turn attribution completes in 1s on a single GPU, remaining stable as context accumulates to 40 turns; and (iv) concept-drift detection is conservative (0% false compaction) with recall bounded by attribution accuracy. We further describe the concept-drift micro compaction design and an interactive incident-tracing/memory-cleaning case study. A companion patent application covers the lineage construction method.

tokenizers v1: encode, decode and scaling, measured

📅 21 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1571 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the tokenizer has not historically been the bottleneck within ML workflows.
  • As models become faster and workloads scale, that balance begins to shift.
  • This is why we have chosen to heavily focus on performance for the upcoming version 1 of tokenizers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the tokenizer has not historically been the bottleneck within ML workflows. Compute-wise, tokenization is light compared to the heavy modeling happening in the rest of the pipeline. Yet, in some cases, it has rapidly become key to accelerating (or slowing down) your machine learning work.

As models become faster and workloads scale, that balance begins to shift. Training on massive datasets, serving many concurrent requests, or repeatedly processing long inputs can put enough pressure on the tokenizer that it starves the model of data.

This is why we have chosen to heavily focus on performance for the upcoming version 1 of tokenizers. Tokenization should be light and should scale with your workflow. Your GPUs should never sit idle waiting for the CPU to complete its tokenization.

In this article, we look at what makes v1 faster than v0.23, often by tens of times.

This work was entirely possible thanks to the rest of the ecosystem. Tokenization is a very active area of open source work, and libraries such as gigatoken, tiktoken, kitoken, tokie, fastokens, wordchipper and ai-tokenizer, as well as many others, have each pushed on what a fast tokenizer can be. We read that work, and several of the ideas below reached us because another project revealed they were worth trying.

In a recent development, before this refactor, tokenizers was nowhere near the performance it could have had, so contributing to it may not have seemed worth it. With this refactor, we hope to make clear that we intend tokenizers to be a library worth contributing to.

We also thank IBM, NVIDIA, and the ExecuTorch team for contributing patches and helping us test across a wide range of hardware to broaden platform support.

We showcase results for the release candidate of tokenizers v1 against other widely used alternatives. We go over single-threaded, multi-threaded, scaling across threads, per-model comparison, per-language comparison, latency, decoding throughput, memory heap, as well as crate size.

We run this from the tokbench repository, and add a command to rerun the benchmarks on your hardware if you would like to do so.

v1 will produce the same token IDs as v0.23. The goal was to preserve the output, the API, the vocabulary and the merge ranks, and improve everything that can be improved. That includes breadth. The library stays general across tokenizer families rather than specialising on BPE, so v1 loads everything v0.23 loaded.

Recent findings suggest that A tokenizer converts text into the list of integers a model reads. tokenizers runs that conversion in four stages. Normalization applies operations such as lowercasing or Unicode normalization to the raw text. Pre-tokenization splits the text into smaller pieces called pre-tokens. The model turns each pre-token into tokens and maps them to IDs in its vocabulary. Post-processing adds any special tokens the model expects.

The model stage is where most of the work described here happens. Eight of the ten model families measured in this article use byte pair encoding, or BPE. BPE starts from the bytes of a pre-token and repeatedly joins the highest ranked adjacent pair until no ranked pair remains. The ranking is learned when the tokenizer is trained and ships with it, so the same text always produces the same IDs. A merge never crosses a pre-token boundary. The other two families use WordPiece and Unigram, the two other model types the library supports.

Industry observers note that the tokenization pipeline page documents the four stages. Tokenization algorithms documents BPE, WordPiece and Unigram.

Industry observers note that each stage was worked on. These are the changes that mattered:.

BPE models use a regular expression to split the input text into smaller, easier to process chunks called pre-tokens. Merges happen inside a pre-token and never across the boundary between two of them, so this split decides what the rest of the pipeline sees.

That regular expression is a fixed parameter of the model. It ships with the tokenizer and never changes at runtime, so there is no need for a general-purpose regex engine to interpret it on every encode. An equivalent splitting function can be written by hand, once, for the pattern a given model actually uses.

Sources indicate that A hand-written function can then use the SIMD instructions (single instruction, multiple data) of a modern CPU, which apply one operation to many bytes at once and suit UTF-8 text well. bitcannon views the input's bytes as parallel streams of bits, so boundaries fall out of boolean operations across whole registers instead of a scan that advances one character at a time. It decides 64 bytes per register operation. The same idea drives Parabix for text processing and simdjson for JSON.

According to recent reports, this depends on recognising the pattern. A handful of grammars cover most byte-level BPE models, and a tokenizer whose pattern is not among them keeps the regex path and none of this speed-up. That is why the gains above vary as much as they do.

Real text contains many repeated words. Because BPE always produces the same token IDs for a given pre-token, v1 can save the result after processing it once. A thread-local cache maps each pre-token's bytes to its token IDs, allowing later occurrences to skip the merge process.

Recent findings suggest that naturally, as the input grows, the number of unique words can grow more slowly than the total number of words. Repeated words then account for an increasing share of the input. Fresh words still appear, which accounts for the occasional misses in the animation below.

Reproduce the shared-prefix result with:.

Industry observers note that caching works best when the input contains repeated pre-tokens. Input with few repeated pre-tokens can pay for lookups without receiving many hits.

It has been revealed that the next major cost comes from the BPE merge loop. For each pre-token, the loop repeatedly finds the highest-priority adjacent pair and merges it. The previous implementation allocated upcoming memory for every call and built a new priority queue for every pre-token.

v1 reuses a scratch buffer owned by the caller, removing those repeated allocations. It stores symbols in a flat array and links adjacent symbols by their positions in that array, which makes updates during merging cheaper. It also processes a batch of pre-tokens in a single model call.

Sources indicate that each candidate pair is also packed into a single 64-bit value, with the merge rank in the high bits. Comparing two candidates is then just comparing two integers, and "no merge here" is the largest possible value, so the loop finds its next merge without a branch.

Small differences in benchmark design can produce large differences in tokenizer performance. We used the following rules to keep the comparison consistent across engines.

Repeatedly encoding one document can be faster than encoding a stream of distinct documents on the same build. The first approach measures performance when the entire document is already represented in the cache. The second measures performance on upcoming input while allowing previously seen pre-tokens to remain cached.

Industry observers note that both conditions are sometimes described as "warm," even though they measure different workloads. Our headline results use distinct documents, and the complete corpus is too large to fit in the cache. Tokenizer benchmarks should identify which workload they use because the choice can dominate the result.

In a recent development, across the ten model families v1's encode path covers, it encodes text 3 to 30 times faster than v0.23 with one thread on an Apple M4 Max. The low end is t5-base, the high end gpt2. It scales at 76% of linear across eight workers. Throughout these changes, v1 produces exactly the same token IDs as the released library.

Sources indicate that the overall improvement comes from several changes working together: a hand-written splitter in place of a regex engine, a cache that answers a repeated word without merging it again, a merge loop that never touches the allocator, and one model call per batch of pre-tokens instead of one per pre-token. Each reduces the work done at a different point in the pipeline.

The next priority is support for more model families. We will move additional models onto the upcoming merge loop before 1.0.0. Once the release candidates stabilize, the next step will be bringing about the improvements within the transformers library and the rest of the ecosystem which depend on the tokenizers library.

This post is generated from tokbench results and will be updated as support expands.

A release candidate for v1 is on crates.io. The API you call is the one you already call, so the only thing that changes is which build you install.

Training is behind a default-on feature that pulls a C++ dependency with it. If you only need to encode, turn it off to exclude the training implementation:.

Encoding is unchanged: same call, same ids.

In a recent development, every figure in this post was measured against this crate. The Python bindings wrap the same code and are built from bindings/python, but they add per-call overhead that none of these measurements include.

The benchmarks in this post cover the completed release-candidate work listed first. The remaining sections show what is still required for 1.0.0 and what we proposal to explore afterward.

This work is in the Rust pre-release on crates.io:.

AWS Marketplace Metering Service now supports decimal usage quantities

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (159 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that AWS Marketplace Metering Service now supports decimal usage quantities in the MeterUsage and BatchMeterUsage APIs.
  • It has been revealed that sellers can price and meter in the units that match how customers consume their product, for example reporting 1.5 terabytes (TB) of storage instead of 1 or 2 TB.
  • This newly introduced feature is available in all AWS Regions where AWS Marketplace Metering Service is available.

Recent findings suggest that AWS Marketplace Metering Service now supports decimal usage quantities in the MeterUsage and BatchMeterUsage APIs. Previously, AWS Marketplace sellers reported usage to both APIs in whole numbers, and now they can report usage with up to six decimal places.

It has been revealed that sellers can price and meter in the units that match how customers consume their product, for example reporting 1.5 terabytes (TB) of storage instead of 1 or 2 TB. To report decimal quantities, sellers use the new UsageQuantityAsDecimal parameter in MeterUsage and QuantityAsDecimal parameter in BatchMeterUsage, and existing integrations that report whole numbers continue to work without changes. Usage allocations, which split reported usage into buckets by tags, also support decimal quantities with the new AllocatedUsageQuantityAsDecimal parameter.

This newly introduced feature is available in all AWS Regions where AWS Marketplace Metering Service is available. To learn more, see MeterUsage and BatchMeterUsage in the AWS Marketplace API Reference.

Towards Data-Efficient, Real-Time World Models

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (203 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.22497v1 Announce Type: fresh Abstract: State-of-the-art world models have been used to produce sequences of gameplay that accord with provided user-input actions. However, high quality, consistent gameplay generation often comes at the cost of inference speed, making real-time interactive play and ideation challenging. The substantial quantities of data used to train state-of-the-art models have also made custom training of these models appear impractical, limiting many of their potential uses in creative fields. In this work we demonstrate a major step towards efficient world models: achieving both fast high-quality inference, and improved data efficiency. This is done by replacing the next-token prediction paradigm with a two-stage discrete diffusion-based approach, introducing a lightweight refinement transformer which carries out iterative masked predictions. Building on an autoregressive world model capable of generating highly consistent and complex sequences over minutes (Kanervisto et al., 2025), we achieve substantial model speed-up (79x) with a modest quality trade-off. Additionally, we demonstrate that this model can be trained to reproduce high-quality, consistent gameplay using a dataset containing approximately one day (28 hours) of gameplay data. Our results demonstrate progress towards removing barriers to the use of world models in settings where real-time inference and data efficiency are essential.

DARWIN: a Geospatial Foundation Model for Marine Intelligence

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (172 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.22496v1 Announce Type: latest Abstract: We present DARWIN, a geospatial foundation model for marine intelligence. Recent Earth-observation foundation models have concentrated on terrestrial domains. The marine realm poses distinct challenges: missingness, multi-modal physical and biogeochemical variables, sparse labels, and dynamics that are transient, multi-scale, and non stationary over time. DARWIN adapts a masked-autoencoder backbone to these properties through missingness-aware encoding, expanded spatial and temporal masking, and Fourier-style positional embeddings, and is pretrained on 26 years of global Copernicus reanalysis together with GEBCO bathymetry. On predicting chlorophyll-a, the pretrained backbone attains the lowest monthly relative error in every month of 2022, outperforming both no-encoder baselines and an identically architected random-init encoder. At 10% of the supervised training data, DARWIN already surpasses the random-init model trained on 100% of the data. Embedding analysis and qualitative reconstructions show that DARWIN captures coherent oceanographic structure rather than memorising input statistics, providing a scalable backbone for downstream marine applications such as anomaly detection, species distribution modelling, and environmental monitoring.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • MLX is Apple's framework for local AI, especially optimized for Apple Silicon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, we are super excited to welcome Jun as our newest team member 🔥. We are completely invested in local AI, and MLX is a central piece of the ecosystem. We are delighted that Jun chose us to set up home and continue contributing to MLX.

MLX is Apple's framework for local AI, especially optimized for Apple Silicon. We are massive MLX supporters since it was the Christmas present from Awni and Angelos in 2023, and proud that Hugging Face is the Hub where people find MLX models and contribute their own. Usage of open, local AI is accelerating, and we believe in a healthy ecosystem where people can find the tools that work for them.

Sources indicate that stability, and hopefully faster development! Graduating from a side job to a fully maintained and funded project will allow Jun to better guide the contributors and build for the long-term. oMLX stays Apache 2.0, and Jun keeps leading it as before.

Our end goal is to unblock the community to run local AI in any shape or form, and provide the tools and building blocks to make that happen. We expect oMLX to serve as a testbed for fresh ideas, while leveraging the foundational work of the dependencies it already relies upon, such as mlx-lm or mlx-vlm. We believe that strong modeling and inference libraries help the community, so we'd love to upstream work to wherever it makes sense. We have been collaborating with many projects mlx-lm, mlx-vlm, LMStudio, and we hope we can strengthen the relationship with Cheng, Prince, Yagil, and their teams to better serve the community together.

Sources indicate that concretely, one focus area is the quick transition from a transformers model definition to a reference MLX implementation that can be consumed by different engines, so each one can focus on the unique features they provide. The transformers library has become the reference for ML model definitions, we want to streamline the process to make upcoming transformers models run on MLX.

We are incredibly excited about the future.

Tech Report: Set up, connect, and govern AI agents faster with Amazon WorkSpaces

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (570 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that building AI agents has become essential.
  • Earlier this year, we launched Amazon WorkSpaces for AI agents, extending the power and security of a cloud work environment to agents, not just people.
  • Industry observers note that setup used to mean configuring the machine by hand.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that building AI agents has become essential. Across your organization, teams want agents to handle ERP transactions, work through a claims queue, and operate the same applications your people use every day. But how do you move from experiments to production? Before an agent touches real systems and real data, you need to verify who it acted on behalf of, what it did, and whether it stayed within the limits you set. Without that visibility, the agent stays stuck in testing, and the value is never realized.

Earlier this year, we launched Amazon WorkSpaces for AI agents, extending the power and security of a cloud work environment to agents, not just people. Today, we're excited to announce new capabilities that make it even easier to operate agents confidently across your enterprise and move them from proof of concept to governed production in fewer steps. You can set up new agents or connect the ones your builders have already built, run them under your own identity providers and policies, and keep a record of everything they do. You don't need to stitch together new tools or build custom monitoring.

Industry observers note that setup used to mean configuring the machine by hand. Now, you can just describe what your agent needs to your AI coding assistant such as Claude Code, Codex, and Kiro. Guided by AWS MCP skills, the assistant builds the WorkSpace from defaults you can adjust. If your teams build on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, you can connect an agent directly with your AWS credentials and skip writing any agent code. Fresh tools also reduce agent costs and increase accuracy by letting an agent carry out a series of actions in a single call and use the computer-use actions its model already knows.

But an agent that can work is not necessarily an agent you can trust with mission-critical work and sensitive data. This release gives you the same oversight over an agent that you have over the employees you manage. First, agents can now sign in through any identity provider (IdP) that supports OIDC, in addition to the existing SAML support. Administrators can send sign-in straight to their IdP, so consumers authenticate with their usual corporate credentials, and you don't build custom authentication. Second, with on-behalf-of (OBO) sign-in, an agent works as the signed-in user, with that user's existing directory identity, permissions, and Group Policies on the desktop.

Recent findings suggest that workSpaces now offers session replay, giving you a reviewable record of what your agent did. Session replay turns session screenshots into a video and pairs it with a plain-language transcript of the agent's actions. Both are stored in your own Amazon S3 bucket and encrypted with your own keys. Your security team can see what the agent saw, and your compliance team gets evidence to support audits.

Together, these updates help move agents out of pilots and into real production scale. Your teams can keep working the way they do today, with agents working alongside them in familiar and trusted cloud work environments. And every one of those agents is held to the same identity, policy, and audit standards as the rest of your workforce. With WorkSpaces, you can bring AI agents into your business without rebuilding decades of software or needing a separate environment to govern them.

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.22490v1 Announce Type: latest Abstract: Language models are increasingly being used as agents capable of planning and executing projects, as well as refining their actions through feedback. This shift raises a question: can current agents complete projects like real scientists? To examine this question, we introduce SciWorkBench, a benchmark for evaluating agents' abilities on real science tasks across biology, chemistry, materials science, and physics. SciWorkBench is built from peer-reviewed literature or expert-contributed research scenarios. We also propose a unified scientific analysis framework validated by domain experts, which can categorize most tasks in SciWorkBench. Each task covers one or more stages of this framework. We evaluate up-to-date models within the Claude Code and Codex agent frameworks under a unified execution and grading protocol. The best-performing agent achieves a mean score of 57.38, indicating that current agents still struggle with realistic scientific workflows. Our failure analysis identifies three recurring weaknesses at the workflow level: difficulty translating scientific knowledge into task-specific procedures, weak integration of evidence across different modalities, and limited capacity for scientific self-correction. These findings highlight the importance of workflow-based evaluation for measuring progress toward reliable AI systems for scientific research.

#7798. RehearsalBench: Can AI Predict What Happens When You Change a Manufacturer?

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (282 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

RehearsalBench: Can AI Predict What Happens When You Change a Manufacturer?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (282 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.22480v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Organizations increasingly ask AI systems what will happen if they change how they operate: which work to automate, which team to resize, what a voice agent will do to waiting times. We introduce RehearsalBench, a benchmark that measures whether AI models can diagnose an operation, choose an intervention, and forecast its consequences. Each model is placed in a simulated bank contact center fitted to real call-level records, sees only what a manager would see, and submits a blueprint and forecasts that are then played out across 200 seeded futures and three plausible versions of the organization. Decisions are scored in dollars at the stakeholders' stated valuations; forecasts are scored on the effect of each change relative to doing nothing. Ten models made 280 attempts across 14 organizations. The best model, GPT-6 Astra, improved on doing nothing by 6.8% of the no-change cost and made 77% less forecast error than a forecaster who always predicts no effect. On average, every model forecast the direction of every specified effect correctly, but models erred on the size of the same effects in the same direction, overstating a voice agent's effect on repeat contacts about five-fold. No model ever recommended holding off when doing nothing was the right choice. To test external validity, twelve models forecast 33 real organizational changes with known outcomes. Under verdict rules fixed in advance, the benchmark's forecast ranking agreed with the real-world ranking (Spearman $\rho = 0.92$, 95% lower bound 0.50). We report the result alongside an inconclusive first test, the analysis choices made after outcomes were seen, and evidence that part of the agreement reflects how well models size their uncertainty.

Transformers now runs llama.cpp quants

📅 22 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1580 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We're adding support for running GGUF models efficiently in transformers, so you can use checkpoints sized for your laptop's memory through the familiar transformers APIs.
  • Recent findings suggest that running AI models on your laptop has become much easier, and llama.cpp has been a significant part of that.
  • In a recent development, this is where we are right now.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We're adding support for running GGUF models efficiently in transformers, so you can use checkpoints sized for your laptop's memory through the familiar transformers APIs. Pick a GGUF from the Hub, load it with from_pretrained, and start generating on your own machine.

Recent findings suggest that running AI models on your laptop has become much easier, and llama.cpp has been a significant part of that. Its inference engine powers local AI tools such as Ollama, LM Studio, and Jan. Alongside projects like MLX, it has helped make local inference a practical option for everyday use.

A recent example of what local AI can feel like:.

In a recent development, this is where we are right now. And i’m not gonna lie it feels pretty magical 🧙‍♀️Qwen3.6 27B running inside of Pi coding agent via Llama.cpp on the MacBook ProFor non-trivial tasks on the @huggingface codebases, this feels very, very close to hitting the latest Opus in Claude… pic.twitter.com/lsIxLoUneU.

GGUF, developed by the llama.cpp team, is a widely used format for local inference. The team also shares quantized checkpoints under ggml-org on the Hub. Publishers such as Unsloth, LM Studio Community, and bartowski also provide ready-to-use GGUF checkpoints in a range of quantizations, so consumers can pick the version that fits their machine. GGUF models have been downloaded millions of times.

Industry observers note that we want to make it easier to run these models locally with transformers, too. Compatibility is only useful if the model is pleasant to run. To bring performance close to llama.cpp, we're reusing its underlying ggml kernels through the kernels library, and reducing overhead in generate. Our initial focus is local inference on Apple Silicon, starting with the Qwen3.5 architecture.

In a recent development, GGUF packages model weights and metadata, including tokenizer information and an optional chat template, in one file. It supports different quantization levels, letting you trade some precision for a smaller memory footprint. Variants such as Q4_K_M mix tensor precisions, using mostly 4-bit weights while keeping sensitive tensors at higher precision.

Here's how quantization changes the file size of Unsloth's Qwen3.5-4B:.

In a recent development, we suggest starting with Q4_K_M, then trying Q5_K_M or Q6_K if you have more memory available. More aggressive quantization can help larger models fit, but the quality tradeoff depends on the model and the task. Evaluate it on the work you actually want the model to do. The Hub's GGUF documentation describes the available quantization types.

To load a GGUF model, pass its Hub model_id and filename as gguf_file to from_pretrained.

No extra configuration is needed: when the weights stay packed on Metal, transformers automatically loads the compatible ggml/Metal layer kernels and uses ggml-org/ggml-attn as the attention implementation. If that kernel cannot be fetched, the model falls back to "sdpa" with a warning, and you can always force "sdpa" by passing attn_implementation="sdpa" explicitly. See the GGUF documentation for more loading options.

That is the only GGUF-specific step. Everything after it is the standard transformers API:.

Without a compatible quantization kernel, the loader falls back to dequantizing the model and uses more memory.

You can also use the same checkpoint with transformers serve, which exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:.

The model argument uses :.gguf: before the colon is the Hub repository (unsloth/Qwen3.5-4B-GGUF), and after it is the file to load (Qwen3.5-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf). This selects a specific quantization from a repository that may contain several.

Industry observers note that for models whose chat template supports thinking, add --reasoning off to skip it or --reasoning on to enable it. The default, --reasoning auto, follows the chat template’s default. See the reasoning options for details.

You can connect a client such as Jan or Pi by adding a custom OpenAI-compatible provider with these settings:.

It has been revealed that transformers runs the model on your Mac, while the client provides the conversation interface. The same endpoint can be used by other clients that support this API.

According to recent reports, our reference for local inference performance is llama.cpp. The comparison below focuses on three GGUF checkpoints: a small dense model, a larger dense model, and a mixture-of-experts model.

The llama.cpp column comes from the llama-bench tool (build 5f55650a7, release b10200, Metal backend from ggml 0.18.0), run as llama-bench -m -p 0 -n 128 -r 3, which reports tg128: the token-generation rate over 128 decoded tokens, averaged across three repetitions, with prompt processing excluded. The transformers column is generate producing the same 128 tokens from a 12-token prompt, best of three warmed runs, and it includes prefill.

Measured on a MacBook Pro M2 Max, 32 GB unified memory, macOS 26.6, PyTorch 2.12.1, kernels 0.17.0, plugged in.

According to recent reports, transformers is close to llama.cpp across all three checkpoints. The chart uses the same measurements described above; it does not imply identical benchmark conditions, since the Transformers measurement includes prefill while llama-bench reports decode-only throughput.

Industry observers note that when GGML and llama.cpp joined Hugging Face, we described their complementary roles: llama.cpp provides a foundation for local inference, while transformers provides a foundation for model definition. GGUF support brings those two closer together.

llama.cpp remains our recommended engine when your priority is efficient local inference. Its dedicated runtime, memory management, and broad hardware support are built around that goal. This integration gives developers a convenient way to work with the same GGUF checkpoints inside transformers:.

For that last case, use GgufConfig(dequantize=True):.

The bigger opportunity is bringing ggml's performance to models that llama.cpp does not support.

Industry observers note that transformers already provides the PyTorch implementations of these architectures. With ggml kernels and quantization schemes available in PyTorch, we can work toward accelerating their supported operations without first implementing the entire model in llama.cpp. This is especially useful for new architectures, research models, and custom variants that may never receive a dedicated llama.cpp implementation.

That opportunity extends beyond the GGUF format itself. A kernel operates on tensors; it does not require the whole model to come from a GGUF file. The same building blocks can be integrated into other transformers models and loading workflows. This also opens a path to other modalities: computer vision models, audio models, and multimodal models could reuse compatible attention, normalization, and matrix multiplication kernels without first having a full implementation in llama.cpp. Each architecture still needs integration and validation; the initial GGUF examples here cover text generation.

Recent findings suggest that we also wanted to show how far we can get while keeping the model and generation loop in Python. With the right kernels and an efficient generation loop, Python and PyTorch can deliver strong local inference performance. The kernels handle the heavy computation, while the generation loop keeps the GPU busy by avoiding unnecessary synchronization.

Our focus was to make eager execution fast without requiring torch.compile. For interactive use, we wanted a quick start and a steady stream of tokens, without compilation pauses or recompilation when input shapes change. The two main pieces of that work are the kernels and generate itself.

Industry observers note that A kernel is a small program that performs an operation on the GPU. PyTorch supplies general-purpose implementations; a specialized kernel can do less work, combine several operations, or read quantized weights directly in their stored format.

It has been revealed that the kernels library lets us distribute compatible builds of ggml's Metal kernels on the Hub and call them from transformers. That brings ggml's work into the PyTorch model without replacing the model with a separate inference runtime.

Sources indicate that the first four packages build on ggml's kernels; the top-k kernel addresses a separate bottleneck in MoE routing. Together they reduce the GPU work needed for each generated token.

To show the contribution of the layer kernels, we compare the same packed GGUF checkpoints with and without them. The quantization kernel stays enabled in both configurations: disabling it would also change how weights are represented and would measure a different tradeoff.

Faster kernels only help if the GPU has work to do. During generation, the CPU schedules GPU operations and controls the loop that produces the next token. Reading a result back from the GPU can force the CPU to wait until queued operations finish. Repeating even a small wait for every token can noticeably reduce throughput.

Two changes address this in generate, which results in improvements for all transformers models (not just when running GGUF files):.

Recent findings suggest that these changes improve the generation loop around the model, so their usefulness extends beyond GGUF. They complement the kernel work: kernels reduce the cost of an operation, while fewer synchronization points let CPU scheduling and GPU execution overlap.

These measurements keep all layer kernels enabled; the bars isolate the changes to the generation loop.

It has been revealed that the initial target is a single interactive conversation on Apple Silicon. There are a few boundaries to keep in mind:.

If you have a GGUF model you would like to use in transformers, open an issue with the checkpoint and your use case. That will help us prioritize support for the models people are running locally.

We are grateful to Sayak Paul, the llama.cpp team, and Bertrand Chevalier for their help integrating the kernels. We also thank Aritra Roy Gosthipaty and Pedro Cuenca for reviewing this blog post, and Lysandre Debut for overseeing the project.

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (414 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that AWS Key Management Service (KMS) now integrates with AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM), giving you a simpler and more consistent way to share KMS keys across your AWS accounts, within your organization in AWS Organizations, and with specific IAM roles and customers.
  • Sharing KMS keys through RAM makes enabling cross-account access faster to set up and safer to maintain.
  • This enhancement is built on latest AWS RAM capabilities that are available for every resource type RAM supports.

Industry observers note that AWS Key Management Service (KMS) now integrates with AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM), giving you a simpler and more consistent way to share KMS keys across your AWS accounts, within your organization in AWS Organizations, and with specific IAM roles and customers. You can now let trusted parties define the access they need through reusable managed permissions in RAM, while keeping full control of your keys and key policies. To share a key, create a resource share by selecting the keys to share, choosing a managed permission, and specifying the principals. You can use AWS managed permissions for common scenarios, or customer managed permissions (CMPs) authored by you or by trusted parties such as SaaS providers and central security teams.

Sharing KMS keys through RAM makes enabling cross-account access faster to set up and safer to maintain. The trusted parties who need access to your keys can publish the policy once as a CMP, without the need for you to modify the key policies by hand. You simply fill in the values that scope it to your environment and attach it to the resource share. Your existing key policy is untouched, so you are always in control of your key as your environment grows. When a new policy version is available via an updated CMP, you decide when to apply it to your resource shares.

This enhancement is built on latest AWS RAM capabilities that are available for every resource type RAM supports. CMPs now support multiple policy statements and additional IAM condition operators, including StringNotEquals, BoolIfExists, and ArnLike, along with the ForAnyValue and ForAllValues prefixes, so you can express precise, least-privilege access. The parameterized managed permissions lets you place a temporary placeholder in CMPs that allows each resource share owner to customize and scope down CMPs to their environment, enabling CMPs to be reused and serve many accounts. CMPs can now be published and shared across accounts, so the authors can maintain one permission, manage its versions centrally, and see every resource share that uses it, while other accounts can use it directly without keeping their own copy.

Recent findings suggest that KMS key sharing with RAM is available in all AWS Regions where both services are available, except the Middle East (UAE) and Middle East (Bahrain). For more information, see Sharing KMS keys with AWS RAM in the AWS KMS Developer Guide and Working with shared AWS resources in the AWS RAM Developer Guide.

PACD: Provenance-Aware Consensus Decoding for Mitigating Cross-Modal Hallucinations in Omnimodal Large Language Models

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (211 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.22456v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Omnimodal large language models (Omni-LLMs) integrate audio, video, and text for multimodal reasoning, yet remain vulnerable to cross-modal hallucinations, where one modality improperly influences predictions about another. Existing training-free decoding methods mitigate these errors through modality perturbation or relevance-based weighting. However, due to interference from irrelevant modality cues during fusion and difficulty detecting shared errors, these methods may suppress correct unimodal predictions and allow erroneous consensus to persist. To address these limitations, we propose Provenance-Aware Consensus Decoding (PACD), a training-free framework for mitigating cross-modal hallucinations. PACD comprises two complementary paths based on whether the branches reach consensus. For non-consensus cases, Relevance-Guided Candidate Arbitration identifies task-relevant unimodal evidence and selectively arbitrates between predictions using alternative candidates. For consensus cases, Provenance-Based Consensus Recovery leverages the outranking principle to evaluate the consistency and strength of layer-wise modality evidence for alternative answers, selectively resolving erroneous consensus under confidence constraints. Extensive experiments on four Omni-LLMs and five benchmarks across two tasks demonstrate the superiority of PACD. Compared to existing methods, PACD achieves up to 27.6% relative improvement over standard decoding across CMM, AVHBench, and SVHalluc for cross-modal hallucination mitigation, and an average relative improvement of 7.7% over best baseline across OmniVideoBench and FutureOmni for general audio-visual reasoning.

arXiv:2611.22432v2 Announce Type: latest Abstract: Fast System-1 models enable responsive actions but struggle with complex or unfamiliar tasks. Large language model (LLM)-based System-2 provides strong reasoning capabilities, yet repeated invocation incurs substantial latency and computational costs. To bridge this gap, we propose JevRSI, a System-1/System-2 collaboration framework that transforms LLM reasoning into transferable decision support through recursive harness improvement. A Jev-style System-1 model enables low-latency action selection, while an asynchronous System-2 LLM develops a modular harness. The harness integrates procedures, state memory, and world models to provide decision contexts spanning the past, present, and future. Utility-driven retrieval selects modules based on both contextual relevance and their utility on previous tasks. Environmental feedback guides targeted revisions and enables recursive self-improvement. Experiments across three datasets show that JevRSI consistently improves decision quality, matching or surpassing LLM agents in several settings. It preserves low-latency execution with favorable performance-cost trade-offs. Moreover, System-2 development interventions decrease as the harness evolves, amortizing System-2 costs through continuous improvement. Our project is available at https://github.com/usail-hkust/JevRSI.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The EvalEval Coalition is thrilled to share that the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) is using EvalEval's infrastructure to openly share evaluation results, supporting more reproducible and verifiable evaluation science.
  • AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema.
  • In a recent development, as AI deployment accelerates, evaluations are becoming increasingly important sources of evidence about model and system performance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The EvalEval Coalition is thrilled to share that the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) is using EvalEval's infrastructure to openly share evaluation results, supporting more reproducible and verifiable evaluation science.

AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema. This next phase of the collaboration puts that shared infrastructure into practice.

In a recent development, as AI deployment accelerates, evaluations are becoming increasingly important sources of evidence about model and system performance. Yet results are reported across many formats, platforms, and outlets, often without enough information to reproduce them. Running the evaluations again may itself be prohibitively expensive.

EvalEval's mission is to improve this ecosystem through a shared reporting schema, Every Eval Ever, and an open platform, Evaluation Cards, that brings evaluation results and the information needed to interpret them into a common structure.

In a recent development, this builds naturally on AISI's work to make evaluation more efficient through OptStop, more statistically rigorous through HiBayES, and more standardised in areas including transcript analysis and capability elicitation. Together, AISI and EvalEval are working to diagnose gaps in evaluation reporting and build shared infrastructure to close them.

It has been revealed that transcript-level transparency matters not only for reproducibility, but also for analysis and diagnosis. In this latest phase of the collaboration, AISI is making publicly reported evaluation methods and findings available through Evaluation Cards where appropriate. The release includes verified results, context, and configuration information for the five benchmarks in the paper's main experiment:.

These results cover six frontier models: Claude Opus 4, Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5, GPT-5.2, and GPT-5.4. The release also includes results from two related cyber evaluations—Cyber CTFs and The Last Ones—which use a different, partially overlapping set of models. The data accompany AISI's paper, How Inference Compute Shapes Frontier LLM Evaluation, which studies how benchmark performance depends on inference-time compute and evaluation protocol.

Performance on Humanity's Last Exam changes with evaluation protocol and inference compute. Each curve demonstrates the cumulative share of attempted tasks solved within a given token count, using the earliest observed success per task. When models received correctness feedback from an oracle after each attempt, they continued to solve additional tasks as token use increased.

It has been revealed that when results are openly released with setup information, researchers and practitioners can examine individual studies more closely and compare findings across the wider ecosystem. Where other reports lack these details, releases like AISI's provide verified reference points for interpreting evaluations in context—for example, by helping researchers understand how setup choices may influence reported performance. As more evaluators adopt EEE, open comparisons like these can support broader and more reliable meta-research.

AISI's Terminal-Bench 2.0 results alongside other reported evaluations for the same models, under different evaluation setups.

We are excited about this adoption and look forward to further standardising and sharing evaluations with AISI and other AI evaluation organisations.

According to recent reports, the EvalEval Coalition is a research community developing scientifically grounded research and robust deployment infrastructure for the evaluation ecosystem. Its goal is to improve evaluation science, address the lack of consensus around documenting evaluation applicability and utility, and broaden coverage of the impacts that matter for scientific research and policy analysis.

The coalition's flagship projects include Every Eval Ever, a shared schema and repository for evaluation results, and Evaluation Cards, which combines benchmark metadata, evaluation-run data, and model metadata into interpretable records. Together, they make it easier to understand when apparently similar scores were produced under meaningfully different conditions.

The UK AI Security Institute is a research organisation within the UK government's Department for Science, Innovation and Technology. Its mission is to equip governments with a scientific understanding of the risks posed by advanced AI. AISI conducts research and builds infrastructure to understand advanced AI capabilities and impacts, develop and test mitigations, and inform policy.

The line that matters for practitioners is quiet: apparently similar scores can be produced under meaningfully different conditions.

It has been revealed that once you've watched a benchmark move just by changing inference-time compute or the elicitation protocol, "Model A beat Model B on X" without a card is marketing, not comparison. Evaluation Cards that ship verified results with configuration — especially transcript-level context where it's appropriate — are how eval becomes a contract instead of a leaderboard screenshot.

One ask I'd put to teams adopting EEE: which fields get skipped first under deadline pressure (seed, tool access, attempt budget, oracle feedback), and do you treat a missing field as "do not cite the delta" rather than "assume defaults"?

Recent findings suggest that reproducible reporting won't remove disagreement. It will make the disagreement about the right variables.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, reinforcement Learning environments give new capabilities to agentic AI systems, and they’re a great way to measure and improve performance in your agents.
  • An environment gives an agent a task, responds to its actions with observations, and scores the outcome.
  • Industry observers note that an RL environment on the Hub is a dataset repo that demonstrates up in the new RL Environments filter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, reinforcement Learning environments give new capabilities to agentic AI systems, and they’re a great way to measure and improve performance in your agents. Therefore, Hugging Face Hub now has a special place for RL Environments.

An environment gives an agent a task, responds to its actions with observations, and scores the outcome. The resulting rewards can measure an agent's performance during evaluation or provide a learning signal during training. For an introduction to this interaction loop, see our blogpost on environments. Within the environment, the agent will perform a set of tasks that are represented as datasets. Therefore, environments can be split into broadly two parts: tasksets and runtimes. In this release, we are focusing on the tasksets.

Industry observers note that an RL environment on the Hub is a dataset repo that demonstrates up in the new RL Environments filter. The Use this dataset button gives you the command to run it in that framework. There is no new repo type, no registry, and no sign-up. There are already environments in Harbor, Verifiers, and NVIDIA NeMo Gym.

In a recent development, every RL paper or framework uses its own way to find environments. Custom hubs, runtime registries, independent task datasets, or a GitHub list of tasks with a custom loader. This means that many of the published environments are siloed: if you publish an environment for one framework, users of the other three can’t load it. If you want to train on an environment from another framework or a new paper, you’ll need to port it by hand.

We think this is the wrong shape. An environment is tasks, tests, containers, and a reward rule, which are data with a runtime on top. The Hub already stores data, versions it, gates it, previews it, and serves it to millions of people. It does not need a second system to hold environments. It needs a way to say "this data is an environment, and here is how you run it.".

The frameworks keep doing what they are good at. The Hub does what it is good at, which is hosting, discovery, and versioning. Nobody has to own the catalogue. In fact, catalogues can run on other platforms too, powered by the hub.

The dataset repository hosts your environment files. The framework runs them locally or on a supported cloud backend. Hugging Face Jobs can run cloud workloads, and Hugging Face Sandboxes, built on Jobs, provide interactive command execution. The tags describe compatibility and generate loading commands; adding a tag does not start a job or sandbox.

In a recent development, the RL Environments filter. Go to huggingface.co/datasets?other=rl-environment. Every dataset with the rl-environment tag appears there, whatever framework it works with.

Framework tags. Four environment frameworks are registered as dataset libraries:.

Each framework tag puts the framework's icon on the dataset page and adds a generated snippet to Use this dataset.

A dataset can carry more than one framework tag. That is the point. Tags describe compatibility, and compatibility is not exclusive. Each listed framework must support the files in the repository; adding a tag does not convert them.

Choose the example for your framework and run it in a separate Python environment with the prerequisites listed below.

According to recent reports, harbor can load task directories from a Hub repository. The oracle agent runs the task's reference solution, then the verifier scores the result. It does not call a model.

The viewer shows the task's reward, verifier output, and logs. This checks the task and its reference solution before you try a model agent.

It has been revealed that the Harbor integration of verifiers v1 can run the same task directories in different runtimes, such as Docker. It also supports different harnesses, including a minimal bash harness.

In a recent development, here repo is the full Hugging Face Git URL, while dataset is the name and version in that repo's registry.json. This loader uses Harbor's registry conventions, so a bare Hub repo ID cannot replace both values.

OpenEnv's Harbor integration can run the same task directories with an agent such as OpenCode and return the verifier's reward alongside the agent's trace.

The command downloads the dataset's tasks/ directories, runs one task in Docker, and writes the result. The default connection uses a temporary Gradio tunnel so the sandboxed agent can reach OpenEnv's model proxy. Read the verifier result and the number of model calls:.

A reward of None means no verifier reward was produced; inspect error before interpreting the run as a model failure. This path expects Harbor task directories.

NeMo Gym supports evaluation and RL training: its environments collect trajectories and compute rewards, while a training framework updates model weights. For example, the Structured Outputs dataset pairs prompts with JSON schemas. Its verifier rewards schema adherence; it does not check whether the generated content is factually correct.

The best part is that this gives one repo and one discussion tab where people report broken tasks from all major frameworks. So when an author fixes a bad test, every framework gets the fix on the next pull.

Open your dataset card and add this to the YAML header:.

That is the whole integration. Keep rl-environment, then list every framework that can load your files. If your environment works with a framework we have not registered yet, open a PR to the list of supported libraries.

The docs have the full reference.

We opened PRs to tag some of the environments people already train on. If you maintain one of these, merge the PR and your environment shows up in the filter.

In a recent development, the first version generates one default snippet per framework. Per-config snippets are next, so a repo with several task sets can show the right command for each. After that we will look at structural detection for frameworks with strict layouts. It would also be really cool build custom task UIs, we’ve been experimenting with this here:.

The bigger goal is for framework tagging to be automatic everywhere. OpenEnv already does it on upload. If you maintain Harbor, Verifiers, Nemo Gym, or any other environment framework, add the tags in your push path. It is a few lines, and every environment your owners publish becomes visible to everyone else.

If you train agents, go browse the filter. If you build environments, publish and tag them, whether they cover coding, tool use, games, robotics, or another task. Include the files, a working run command, and the rule that produces the reward so others can use them. If your framework is missing, contribute it to the list of supported libraries.

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.22407v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Robotic applications often rely on long-running operations, such as navigation, manipulation, and inspection, which in ROS~2 are commonly implemented as actions. Unlike topics and services, actions involve a structured lifecycle comprising goal submission and acceptance, feedback, status updates, result retrieval, and cancellation. Existing versions of ROSMonitoring support topics and services, but do not reconstruct this lifecycle or expose action-level events to a runtime-verification oracle. In this paper, we extend ROSMonitoring with runtime monitoring and enforcement for ROS~2 actions. Actions are declared directly in the monitoring configuration and automatically instrumented through the underlying ROS~2 communication endpoints. The generated monitor reconstructs action-level events, correlates them through goal identifiers, maintains the state of active goals, and translates violations into protocol-aware enforcement operations. These include goal rejection, cancellation, message suppression, and protocol-compliant responses generated directly by the monitor when the original communication cannot be forwarded. We evaluate the implementation through controlled stress tests that vary the number of action invocations, workload size, and clientâ€“server topology. The results show approximately linear growth in monitoring cost with repeated action invocations under a fixed workload, while larger action workloads and a greater number of configured clientâ€“server pairs introduce additional overhead. These results characterise the scaling behaviour of the current implementation under the tested sequential workloads while highlighting the main performance limitations of the current synchronous implementation.

Industry News: Symbolic Abstraction Refinement

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (355 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.22404v1 Announce Type: upcoming Abstract: Autonomous systems choose actions whose outcomes are uncertain and are subject to time constraints. Probabilistic timed automata (PTAs) model exactly this, and verifying one answers a question about the system's decision-making: the maximum probability of reaching a goal, or the minimum probability of reaching a hazard, that a controller can guarantee. Verification normally works over symbolic states, each pairing a discrete location with a region of clock values, and its difficulty is that the best behavior generally varies within such a region. The PRISM verifier's most capable PTA method responds by splitting regions until each is uniform, rebuilding the transitions that reach them and propagating the split backward through the state graph of a stochastic game, a cascade of graph reconstruction that partitions regions the property never depends on. We present SYMAR, which instead makes the value function symbolic: each symbolic state carries a function from sub-regions of its clock region to probability bounds, so refinement is the appearance of new sub-regions in that function, and previously generated states are never split nor their incoming transitions reconstructed. Both sources of PTA nondeterminism, the timing and the choice of actions, are captured implicitly by the preimage computation that produces those sub-regions. Heuristic forward search then bounds how much refinement is done at all, expanding an And-Or graph from the initial state along the most promising behaviors so that effort is confined to the property-relevant fragment, guided by bounds and preferred actions from a single unrefined run of the existing method; a partial-refinement backup keeps the otherwise combinatorial sub-region count lean, and every stored interval provably contains the true probability. On the PRISM PTA benchmarks, whose subproblems recur in autonomous systems (distributed agreement under contention, leader election, and self-configuration without central coordination), SYMAR is up to 108x faster, solves an instance on which the existing method exhausts the time limit, and is markedly less sensitive to the deadline constant, resolving one instance in a 37-node search graph, unchanged as the deadline triples, where the existing method needs 86,380 abstract states and 73 refinement rounds.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, holo4 is our latest series of agentic models.
  • Holo4 builds on our previous model and interacts with software through any available interface: GUIs, code, MCP and APIs.
  • Holo4 clicks and types on a screen, writes and runs its own code, and calls MCP or API tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, holo4 is our latest series of agentic models. It comes in two sizes: 27B dense and 35B-A3B Mixture of Experts. Both are available on the H Models API. We are also releasing an updated version of Holotron 3: Holotron4 Nano.

Holo4 builds on our previous model and interacts with software through any available interface: GUIs, code, MCP and APIs. It scores well on academic benchmarks, but we built it for real business workflows. It was trained through supervised and reinforcement learning on a large set of environments and tasks, including those generated by our Agentic Task Factory.

Holo4 clicks and types on a screen, writes and runs its own code, and calls MCP or API tools. It uses whichever fits the task. Most agentic models are trained for one interface only: GUI-focused models are blind without a screen, while models that prefer tool calling are stuck in front of an application that has no API. Real work is not siloed that way, and a single business task can require combining these different approaches.

In a recent development, holo4 runs on desktops, on the web, on Android, in a code sandbox and against business APIs. It is the same model in each case and it is called the same way. You do not need to select a different model for each platform.

Sources indicate that holo4 models improve significantly over their Qwen base. Holo4 trails only the strongest closed models on long workflows: on OSWorld 2.0, Holo4 27B scores 61.7% against 81.8% for Opus 5.5, and Holo4 35B-A3B reaches 30.9%. However, it does so with orders of magnitude fewer parameters and at a much lower cost. We open-source every trajectory behind our scores on public benchmarks: replay each step at trajectories.hcompany.ai or download them from Hugging Face.

On the hardest academic benchmarks for desktop control (OSWorld 2.0) and API use (AutomationBench), Holo4 competes with frontier models at a much lower cost per task.

The same recipe turns Nemotron 3 Nano Omni into Holotron4 Nano, a generalist agentic model that significantly improves over the base model on GUI workflows and in environments exposing MCP, APIs or coding sandboxes.

A 960-execution factorial on 20 initialization seeds compares CAD-feedback and landmark-based recovery from identical post-wait physical states within each holding and waiting condition. Protected completion requires successful recovery under the declared execution constraints. At a 1 s wait with registered wrist references, their protected completion counts change from 6/40 versus 19/40 under registered holding to 34/40 versus 22/40 under position-only holding. Trajectory analysis localizes the main separation to grasp formation: small observation-time target residuals precede large tracking errors. Joint diagnostics and controlled interventions characterize persistent tracking constraints. On fresh seeds, gradual position reanchoring improves CAD recovery's long-wait completion by 42.5 percentage points and reduces mean complete recovery time by 6.06 s relative to registered holding. Additional evaluations with pretrained policies, handover, and a mass-matched geometry characterize holding-reference sensitivity across executors and physical regimes. These findings establish holding reference as an explicit evaluation condition for comparing visual recovery performance.

#7766. Getting the Source Right, Not Just the Fact: Source-Aware Verification for MCP Agents

📅 29 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1849 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Getting the Source Right, Not Just the Fact: Source-Aware Verification for MCP Agents

📅 29 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1849 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, tool-using LLM agents no longer read from a single retrieved passage.
  • Our latest paper, ProvenanceGuard: Source-Aware Factuality Verification for MCP-Based LLM Agents (read it on Hugging Face, or on arXiv in the meantime), targets that gap.
  • Industry observers note that consider a customer support agent that answers, "According to the account record, this plan includes a 30-day refund window." The refund window may be perfectly real, but stated in a policy document, not in the account record the answer points to.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, tool-using LLM agents no longer read from a single retrieved passage. Through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an agent can call a search tool, inspect a structured patient or account record, query a database, and pull metadata, then weave all of it into one answer. That m aakes the usual question of factuality more subtle than it looks. Most of the systems built to check LLM answers, from RAGAS faithfulness to fine-grained checkers like MiniCheck, AlignScore, and SummaC, ask whether a claim is supported by the available evidence once that evidence has been pooled together. In their usual form, they do not tell us which MCP tool output supports each claim, or whether that is the source the answer names.

Our latest paper, ProvenanceGuard: Source-Aware Factuality Verification for MCP-Based LLM Agents (read it on Hugging Face, or on arXiv in the meantime), targets that gap. The failure mode we care about is one we call cross-source conflation: a claim that is true somewhere in the evidence, but attributed to the wrong source. A source-blind verifier may pass it, because the fact does exist in the pool. A source-aware verifier should not.

Industry observers note that consider a customer support agent that answers, "According to the account record, this plan includes a 30-day refund window." The refund window may be perfectly real, but stated in a policy document, not in the account record the answer points to. Pool the two together and the claim looks supported. Keep them separate and the attribution is wrong, and in a data-sensitive setting a wrong attribution can be as damaging as a wrong fact. The same pattern reveals up in a clinical agent, where a patient-specific medication detail taken from a patient-history tool becomes misleading the moment the answer presents it as a finding from the medical literature.

In a recent development, A claim can be supported by one MCP source while the answer attributes it to another. Source-blind scoring sees support in the pooled evidence and passes it; ProvenanceGuard separately checks whether the supporting source matches the one the answer states or implies. Source: paper Figure 1.

In a recent development, this is why faithfulness scores, useful as they are, are not enough for MCP agents. An answer carries provenance, sometimes explicitly ("according to the account record") and sometimes implicitly. ProvenanceGuard keeps that connection between claim and source available for inspection.

Recent findings suggest that provenanceGuard is a post-generation verification layer that sits on top of a black-box MCP agent. It runs after an agent produces an answer, and never collapses the evidence into one anonymous context. Instead it carries the source identity all the way through the pipeline. It reads the captured MCP trace, including the tool outputs and their source IDs, without retraining the agent. Then it does five things in sequence: it breaks the answer into specific claims, finds the source most relevant to each one, checks whether that source actually supports it, compares the source with the one the answer names or implies, and finally emits both a per-claim source verdict and a global, answer-level allow or block decision.

Recent findings suggest that the verification flow. Source identity is preserved through decomposition, routing, support scoring, attribution checking, and repair, rather than being pooled. Blocked answers can go through RARR-style repair and be re-verified. Source: paper Figure 2.

Industry observers note that A few of the design choices are worth calling out. For the experiments in our paper, we used local models so the captured traces could be processed in a controlled, offline setup: MiniLM helps find the relevant source, a DeBERTa NLI verifier model checks whether that source supports the claim, and a local language model helps break answers into claims. The verifier also checks literal values closely: a number, date, or identifier absent from the source cannot pass merely because the sentence sounds plausible. A calibrated decision step combines these signals. If an answer is blocked, a RARR-style repair step can try a source-grounded revision or a safe fallback, which the verifier then checks again.

It has been revealed that those named models are the setup we evaluated, not a requirement of ProvenanceGuard. The same claim, source, and decision steps can be adapted to hosted models where a team prefers cloud services; a newly introduced setup would need its own testing and calibration. Our reported results come from the local configuration. Its conservative decision policy suits data-sensitive review, where getting the source right matters more than producing the fastest possible answer.

Sources indicate that we tested ProvenanceGuard on answers from a medical agent that had used patient records, research articles, and other tools. This gave us 281 real traces to study. Medicine is a useful test because a fact from a patient's record and a fact from general research cannot be treated as the same source. The method can also be used in other fields when an agent keeps a record of its tool outputs and source IDs. For the main test, human experts checked 361 claims from 40 answers set aside from the data used to develop the system.

The most direct result is this: experts remarked 139 claims should not pass, and ProvenanceGuard caught 138 of them. It let one through. It also held 67 claims that the experts considered supported, sending them for review or repair. This reflects the cautious setting we tested: it favors a second look at some supported claims over letting unsupported ones through. For claims with an identifiable source, it also picked the right source about 86% of the time in this test.

We ran four other support checkers on the same claims. ProvenanceGuard scored highest on the paper's measure of how well a system catches claims that should be blocked while avoiding unnecessary blocks. The other checkers in this comparison did not tell us which tool output supported each claim. ProvenanceGuard records that connection, so a reviewer can see the source checked for each claim and the decision it produced.

In a recent development, binary support metrics on the same held-out claim packet. ProvenanceGuard matches or beats the source-blind baselines on blocking while also producing per-claim source verdicts. Source: paper abstract and Table III.

In a separate, harder test with several similar sources, ProvenanceGuard scored 0.846 F1 for deciding which claims to block, but identified the exact source correctly in 50.3% of claims. Telling similar sources apart remains an notable area for improvement.

We also ran a controlled test focused on wrong attribution: we changed the named source in 50 cases while leaving the supporting evidence intact. ProvenanceGuard caught all 50 swaps. This highlights it can detect a clear source error, while the harder test shows the challenge of choosing among many plausible sources.

Blocking is only useful if there is something to do with a blocked answer. Wired to the RARR-style repair loop, the full-trace run resolved all 173 blocked answers, though 144 of them ended in fallback text rather than a substantive rewrite, which is the system choosing to avoid an unverifiable answer rather than manufacture one. On reconstructed multi-source test traces, a fresh repair run resolved all 59 initially blocked answers with only two terminal fallbacks. As an offline gate the overhead is modest, roughly half a second per answer on the reported local configuration, with the NLI and routing calls themselves in the tens of milliseconds.

In a recent development, as agents move from single-passage RAG to multi-tool MCP setups, the question of which source a fact actually came from stops being a footnote and becomes part of what factuality means. ProvenanceGuard makes that source connection visible claim by claim. For Multiverse Computing, that means a way to check existing agents while keeping sensitive traces in a controlled environment when needed. The medical study is one use case; the same approach can be adapted wherever an agent's trace preserves its tools and sources.

Industry observers note that that adaptation is already visible in NVIDIA NVFlow, which merged an optional grounding-verification stage for its finance agent. It checks completed answers against the SEC excerpts the agent retrieved and saves separate decisions without changing the original rollout or training data. The NVFlow contribution uses ProvenanceGuard's source-aware verification approach; the repair loop discussed above belongs to the broader research system.

ProvenanceGuard was also presented as a poster at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 at UC Berkeley.

Industry observers note that want the full technical details, including the routing and NLI derivations, the calibration ablations, the multi-source stress slices, and the complete results tables? Read the full paper on Hugging Face, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying source-aware verification to your own agents.

The failure mode that matters for MCP agents is quieter than "hallucination": a claim that is true somewhere in the pooled tool outputs, attributed to the wrong source.

Source-blind faithfulness can still go green in that case — the fact exists in the soup. Source-aware verification is the contract upgrade: keep tool/source IDs through claim decomposition, support check, and attribution check, then allow/block with a per-claim source verdict a reviewer can actually inspect.

In a recent development, practical ask for teams wiring MCP: when your eval claims "grounded," does it mean supported-by-any-tool-output, or supported-by-the-source-the-answer-named? Those are different release gates. In multi-tool setups the second one is the one that catches cross-source conflation before a human trusts the citation.

It has been revealed that hi, thank you for your comment. You’ve captured the concern well. For ProvenanceGuard, when a claim is “grounded” it means it is supported by the source the answer names or implies. Finding the fact somewhere else in the tool outputs isn’t enough. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon Redshift now supports multi-statement transactions, automatic write-conflict resolution, and time travel for Apache Iceberg tables.
  • In a recent development, with multi-statement transactions, you group several statements in a single BEGIN…COMMIT statement and publish them as one atomic Iceberg snapshot.
  • 1/ Resolving concurrent writes for Apache Iceberg tables using Amazon Redshift.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Amazon Redshift now supports multi-statement transactions, automatic write-conflict resolution, and time travel for Apache Iceberg tables. You can run multi-step, concurrent transformation pipelines directly on Iceberg tables and audit the results, with the transaction semantics you expect from a data warehouse. This helps anyone writing to Iceberg tables at production scale. Batch jobs get all-or-nothing commits across multiple steps. Streaming and scheduled jobs can write to the same tables at the same time. Analysts, auditors, and AI agents can query a table as it existed at any point in time.

In a recent development, with multi-statement transactions, you group several statements in a single BEGIN…COMMIT statement and publish them as one atomic Iceberg snapshot. This means a multi-step load such as a MERGE followed by a DELETE, can be commited together as one atomic operation, are never queryable in a half-applied state, and roll back cleanly if there's a failure. Automatic conflict resolution lets concurrent writes, such as streaming inserts alongside scheduled deletes, write to the same table and commit together when their changes don't overlap, instead of failing and retrying. Time travel lets you query a table as it existed at a past point in time with AS OF TIMESTAMP. You can use it to reproduce reports, audit changes, or recover from a bad write without keeping extra copies. These capabilities are available in all AWS commercial Regions for Amazon Redshift’s provisioned RG or serverless clusters that are writing to or querying Iceberg tables.. To get started, see the following list of resources:.

1/ Resolving concurrent writes for Apache Iceberg tables using Amazon Redshift.

2/ Multi-statement transactions for Apache Iceberg tables in Amazon Redshift.

3/ Time travel support for Apache Iceberg.
