Welcome Beam: a 501B open model you can own, customize, and scale

📅 16 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3330 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face!
  • Beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases.
  • It has been revealed that beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face! It is the first model from the upcoming US lab, Reflection, and it’s open! It's a mixture-of-experts (MoEs) model with 501B parameters (23B active per token), supports text as input, has a context window of 1M tokens, and is released under the Apache 2.0 license.

Beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases. It is for teams that want a frontier-scale model on their own hardware, infrastructure, or cloud, and want to customize it to their own use cases. Beam ships with its own dedicated open source Rust based harness that delivers the best performance from the model.

It has been revealed that beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang. We’ve worked with the Reflection team to bring you inference, SFT (supervised fine tuning), and RL (reinforcement learning) recipes for you to build with this model for your needs. On top of day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM, this post shows you how to run it, how to post-train it, and what we built with it.

Reflection is going to give out $10,000 Hub credits to the best projects that use Beam. All you have to do is make a thing, and share it on the Hub:.

Sources indicate that if you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build the space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. We’ll collect all the links, select the best, and send out the credits to your Hub accounts.

Recent findings suggest that beam is a text-only model built for long-context (1M context length) reasoning and agentic work. It is a sparse MoE model, where each token is computed by a small fraction of the network, so it runs at the speed of a much smaller model while keeping the capacity of a large one.

Industry observers note that the decoder has 52 layers with a hidden size of 5,120. Most layers use sliding-window attention over the previous 512 tokens; every sixth layer, and the last one, attend to the full context. That gives 43 sliding-window layers and 9 global ones.

Inside the attention block (both layer types).

Recent findings suggest that the two kinds of layers handle position differently. Sliding-window layers use RoPE, since relative position matters most within a short window. Global layers use no positional encoding. Instead, each query is multiplied by a scaler that grows slowly with the number of visible tokens, (1 + (pos + 1) / 2048) ** 0.1. It acts as a temperature: the softmax keeps its precision as the context lengthens instead of flattening out. The implementation calls this scalable-softmax query scaling.

According to recent reports, attention uses grouped-query attention with 48 query heads and 8 key-value heads, with RMSNorm on queries and keys. A learned sigmoid gate, computed from the layer input, scales every channel of every head before the output projection.

The first 3 layers use a dense SwiGLU MLP. The other 49 replace it with a Mixture-of-Experts block of 256 experts, each a SwiGLU MLP with an intermediate size of 2,560, or about 39M parameters. The experts hold 98.4% of the model's parameters.

In a recent development, the router follows DeepSeek-V3's group-limited scheme. It scores all 256 experts with a sigmoid, splits them into 8 groups of 32, keeps the 4 best groups (ranked by the sum of each group's top two scores), then picks the top 8 experts inside them. Beam uses the same group sizes as DeepSeek-V3 but no shared expert. Expert outputs are combined with normalized router weights and scaled by 2.5.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 23B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of a 501B model but runs at the speed of a 23B one. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores most parameters in 4-bit precision for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, some parameters are kept in BF16 for accuracy. There are also FP8 checkpoints on the hub which are ideal for Hopper and Ampere series chips.

If you want to deploy Beam yourself, check out the vLLM or SGLang recipes below.

Recent findings suggest that the residual connections are the most distinctive part. A standard transformer adds each sublayer output to the stream with weight 1, so the stream grows with depth.

According to recent reports, beam counts the input embedding as step 1. At step k it adds the sublayer output with weight 1/sqrt(k) and keeps the existing stream with weight sqrt((k-1)/k). The squares of the two weights sum to one, so the stream stays at a constant scale from the first layer to the last. After all 104 additions, every sublayer output and the input embedding carry the same weight in the final hidden state.

Sources indicate that every sublayer is also normalized before and after, and the final logits pass through a tanh softcap at ±30, computed in FP32. The implementation fixes where it computes in FP32: the router, the SwiGLU product, the norms, RoPE, the query scaling and the softcap.

Recent findings suggest that hybrid attention works well for long contexts. Each layer caches 2 x 8 KV heads x 128 dims = 2,048 values per token. If all 52 layers kept every token, the cache would grow by 208 KiB per token. Only the 9 global layers keep the whole sequence. The 43 sliding-window layers hold a fixed 512-token window each and stop growing. So the cache grows by 36 KiB per token, roughly a sixth of the naive rate.

These numbers are per sequence, in BF16, with the transformers dynamic cache.

Here are the benchmark results across different precision levels, as provided by the Reflection team.

The most practical way to serve the model is serving the NVFP4 checkpoint, which retains most of the quality of the bf16 checkpoint. NVFP4 stores some weights in 4 bits, and this way, it shrinks the 501B parameters in BF16 from 1 TB to ~280 GB. Blackwell GPUs run NVFP4 natively but GPUs older than Blackwell like the H200 can't. The FP8 checkpoints are suitable for GPUs older than Blackwell.

According to recent reports, A B200 has 180 GB of HBM3e, so two of them (360 GB) can hold the Beam weights, with little room left for activations and the KV cache. Proposal for four B200s (720 GB), which leaves plenty of room for long contexts and concurrent requests. You can also serve it on a full 8xB200 node, or on two B300s at 288 GB each, or even 8xRTX Pro 6000. If you don't have Blackwell hardware, use Inference Providers (serverless) to test Reflection.

Beam comes with day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM.

Install the latest version of transformers.

The easiest way to run Beam is the text-generation pipeline:.

In a recent development, the pipeline returns the whole chat. The last message is Beam's reply, already parsed by the response template.

Going one level lower, use AutoModelForCausalLM and AutoTokenizer.

Sources indicate that beam's tokenizer carries a response template. parse_response reads it and turns the raw output into a message dict, with the reasoning, the answer, and any tool calls in separate fields. This avoids the usual regex for splitting reasoning from answers from tool calls. And the rules ship with the tokenizer, so the parsed structure matches what Beam was trained to produce. The chat template can pre-write part of the assistant turn, which the parser needs to see.

Pass tools to parse_response as well. Beam writes tool-call arguments inline, in its own XML-style grammar, so a bare 7 could be a number or a string. With the tool schemas, the parser casts each argument to its declared type.

Beam's config defines an expert-parallel plan. Expert parallelism puts each expert on one device. Attention, the dense layers, the embeddings and the LM head are replicated on every device. That is 8B parameters, or 16 GB in BF16. Load the model with a DistributedConfig:.

According to recent reports, launch the script with torchrun across 16 H200 GPUs. Each one then holds 78 GB of weights. With 8 GPUs each would hold 139 GB, which leaves no room on a 141 GB H200. The number of devices must divide the number of experts, 256.

Beam has day-0 support in vLLM. The command below serves the BF16 checkpoint with tensor parallelism across 16 GPUs (two 8x H200 nodes) and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:.

For faster generation, add DFlash2 speculative decoding. A small drafter model proposes up to 15 tokens ahead, and Beam checks them all in one forward pass, so each step can accept several tokens. The cost is a little extra memory for the drafter:.

According to recent reports, both commands start an OpenAI-compatible server, so you can point any OpenAI client at http://localhost:8000/v1. For additional serving configurations, see the proposed Beam recipe for vLLM.

Beam also has day-0 support in SGLang. We recommend serving it with DFlash2 speculative decoding, which both commands below turn on. On Blackwell, the NVFP4 checkpoint fits on 4 B300s:.

On Hopper GPUs, use the FP8 checkpoint on 8 H200s instead. Only three flags change: the checkpoint, the tensor-parallel size (8 instead of 4), and the attention backend (fa3 instead of trtllm_mha, which needs Blackwell):.

Beam is available on Hugging Face Inference Providers, powered by Baseten, Fireworks, and Together, with more to follow soon.

According to recent reports, we are sharing some vibe evals of Reflection Beam-501B-A23B on five tasks, once each at low and high reasoning effort through the Reflection platform. These are vibe evals, not benchmarks. If you’re planning on using Beam, this is a great way to kick the tires and see how it behaves on specific use cases, and importantly, where it wins and loses.

According to recent reports, below is an overview of the prompts we ran and the output traces from the hub. The complete inputs, outputs, API usage, task fixtures, graders and conversation traces are in this public Hugging Face bucket.

In a recent development, * Low's long-context response got all code behavior and all six source citations correct. However, the response did not correspond to the parsers format, so this is partly prompt ambiguity.

† Low returned the correct answer, but omitted the requested justification. High supplied a correct roots-of-unity proof, independently reviewed.

Don’t take our word for it. Dig into the bucket, rewrite for your use case or project and push Beam to the limit.

In a recent development, you can fine tune Beam for your own use cases. Here, we share some examples in TRL and Miles to get you started on supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.

Recent findings suggest that the quickest way to adapt Beam to your own data is supervised fine-tuning with TRL's SFTTrainer. To keep memory manageable, we train LoRA adapters with PEFT rather than updating all 501B parameters: We used TRL’s SFTTrainer to adapt Beam to a simple goal: keep its reasoning in the language requested by the user. We fine-tuned on Multilingual-Thinking with LoRA, which trains a small set of adapter weights while keeping the base model frozen.

The setup combines model sharding at load time, expert parallelism, FlashAttention 4 and sequence packing. LoRA SFT fits on a single node with 8 B300 GPUs, reaching around 19,000 tokens per second. The corresponding H100 setup uses four nodes.

According to recent reports, after one epoch of Multilingual-Thinking, Beam reasoned in the requested language on 16 out of 16 held-out prompts, compared with 3 out of 16 for the base model. This small evaluation measures language adherence, rather than the correctness of the reasoning itself.

Training loss (left) and mean token accuracy (right) during a separate 500-step run on a reasoning subset of open-r1/Mixture-of-Thought, using one 8-GPU B300 node. These training metrics are from the official TRL example PR.

Reflection and RadixArk built a recipe that trains the model with GRPO in Miles, in BF16. You can revision the full model or use LoRA to train adapters while keeping the base weights frozen. Megatron trains, SGLang generates the rollouts, and Miles publishes the new weights to the rollout engines after each update. We reviewed the recipe.

It has been revealed that the recipe runs GRPO on DAPO-Math-17K and evaluates on AIME25. Build the image, download the data, and submit the job to a Ray cluster of twelve 8x H200 nodes:.

Industry observers note that sample: 32 prompts are passed to the model with 8 responses each. Two SGLang engines serve the rollouts on 16 GPUs each.

Score: the boxed answer is checked against the label, with a soft penalty for responses near the length limit.

Patch: one optimizer step on all 256 samples. Group-relative advantages with truncated importance sampling, no KL or entropy penalty.

Train in parallel: tensor parallelism 8, expert parallelism 8, data parallelism 8, with sequence parallelism and full recompute.

Optimizer: Adam at a constant 1e-6. Gradients in BF16, master weights in FP32, moments in BF16. The optimizer state streams through node-local NVMe, so each trainer node needs 2 TB of scratch.

Sources indicate that evaluate: AIME25 every five rollouts, eight samples per problem. A checkpoint is saved every twenty.

In a recent development, the next rollout is generated while the current one trains, so responses are one update behind. Add --resume to continue from the last checkpoint. execute-colocate runs the same recipe on eight nodes, with every GPU training and serving in turn.

Recent findings suggest that you can also run GRPO with LoRA on four 8× H200 nodes: 16 GPUs for training and 16 for rollouts. The recipe trains rank-16 adapters on Beam’s attention, dense MLP, and expert layers while keeping the base weights frozen. Only adapter weights are synchronized with SGLang, and the optimizer state stays in GPU memory, removing the need for NVMe optimizer offloading.

Sources indicate that if you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build a space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. To inspire you, here are a few things we built.

Sources indicate that at Hugging Face we love open and local models that run native to their hardware, but building native apps on Mac can be hard! Let’s see if Beam can help us out.

According to recent reports, we asked Beam to build a native MacOS application that turns speech to text, and conveniently drops it at your cursor. We want to use MLX to get the most out of our Mac Metal and the Parakeet Model for great speech-to-text.

We used Beam with the Pi coding harness to build the initial native macOS menu bar app, running Parakeet with MLX. The saved run includes follow-up prompts; the final source also includes later Codex repairs. The prompt above is a condensed version of the build requirements.

According to recent reports, you can check out the agent trace of how Beam built this in pi in this trace. If you want to try the demo out, download the source code or read the setup instructions.

We wanted to see whether Beam could make faster progress by splitting a programming task across agents. We paired Beam with the open-source Pi coding agent and compared three setups: 1. one agent working alone, 2. five persistent peers collaborating through a shared Git repository, and 3. a lead agent delegating work to asynchronous subagents. The harness ran on Hugging Face jobs with inference through Reflection’s platform API.

In a recent development, for the tasks, we used ProgramBench: agents must recreate a program from its compiled executable and documentation, without seeing its source code or the evaluator’s tests. Each setup had the same 8M API-token ceiling and two-hour solver limit per task, shared across its agents. We saved implementation snapshots and evaluated them against fixed hidden-test suites from the ProgramBench-Tests dataset.

Our score-versus-latency plot indicates the average fraction of tests passed. The time axis uses fixed reference rates for model tokens plus measured tool time, rather than elapsed wall time. We initially ran five tasks. The current figure shows a post-hoc subset of jq, xsv, FIGlet, and hexyl; ripgrep was excluded across all three setups because grading its saved artifacts was too slow. The published results retain all 15 original episodes.

You can inspect the runs in the Trackio dashboard, explore the published result data, and reuse the study harness.

Sources indicate that decision models are all the rage at the moment because they’re super fast and practical for many use cases. We started with Beam in Pi after Beam’s quota ran out to train and evaluate a custom decision model for developer incident triage.

According to recent reports, we wanted to see whether a coding agent could turn an incident-triage policy into a small, fast decision model. The task was to read a developer incident and choose the responsible team, its severity, and whether someone should be pinged immediately. Using Unsloth, we fine-tuned Qwen3.5-0.8B to score these choices directly.

First, the workflow built a synthetic dataset containing 2.3k incidents split by incident cluster for training, calibration, and testing. We trained a LoRA adapter and decision head for three epochs, with a 4-bit backbone, on one H100 80GB on the Science Slurm cluster.

For a baseline, we prompted the unadapted model with the full triage policy and ticket, without examples, and asked it to generate the three decisions as JSON. On the same 320 synthetic test tickets, the fine-tuned decision model got all three answers correct on 76.25%, versus 4.69% for prompted zero-shot. Mean ticket latency fell from 1,218.06 ms to 102.58 ms, an 11.9× speedup.

If you want to try out this experiment for yourself, check out the artifact bucket which contains the data, code, checkpoints and results.

It has been revealed that beam is a 501B open model that you can run on your own hardware and change. Start with the BF16 checkpoint, or try one of the quants FP8, NVFP4. If you build something with Beam, share it in the discussions tab.

Well why don't you build something that can run on cunsumer GPU like Qwen 3.8 Flash Next for example using strata ?

Sources indicate that that’s a good question. Apart from large corporations, no one would be able to set up this model in a way that allows it to function properly—it requires 8 RTX 6000 graphics cards, which would cost around 150,000 euros in total.

According to recent reports, thanks for sharing this! Small nit, but would you be able to add higher resolution diagrams for the model architecture figures? They come out pixelated for me (and possibly others) so I can't read the smaller annotations in the figures.

This is a genuinely exciting release — 501B Apache 2.0 with 1M context is the kind of thing that makes "open" in open-source mean something again. The residual stream design with the 1/sqrt(k) weighting is a nice touch; it's the sort of architectural detail that makes a real difference at scale without being a headline feature.

According to recent reports, one question from the NLP side: the post focuses heavily on coding and agentic use cases, which makes sense for the target audience. But how does Beam handle multilingual text? I'm asking specifically because the 1M context window is exactly what you need for cross-lingual document understanding, and if the training data is skewed toward English + code, that's a gap that matters for non-English research communities.

Also — is the training data or at least the data mixture documented? For a model this size under Apache 2.0, reproducibility of the training setup is part of the open-source promise, and I'd love to see it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Model ML, a London-based personal AI platform for financial and professional services, has secured $250m in a Series B round that values the company at $1.5bn.

Industry observers note that general Atlantic and QED Investors co-led the investment. Evolution Equity Partners, Airtree, Forestay Capital, Y Combinator, FT Partners, Latitude, Inception Fund and 13Books Capital also took part. The deal lifts the total capital raised by Model ML to $350m.

Sources indicate that the raise comes after a period of rapid expansion. Over the third quarter of 2026, annual recurring revenue at the firm increased twelvefold compared with the same period a year earlier, while daily active users rose 26-fold. Model ML plans to put the new capital towards growing its research and engineering headcount in London and New York, with the aim of advancing its product and handling larger customer rollouts. The firm also opened offices this year in Paris, Madrid, Tokyo, Singapore and Dubai so it can support clients across their various locations.

Set up by brothers and serial founders Chaz and Arnie Englander, Model ML provides bankers, consultants and investors with an individual AI agent. The agent learns about each user’s clients, active transactions and preferred ways of working, operates on the firm’s own systems and data, runs continuously and tailors itself further with each use.

Recent findings suggest that rather than waiting to be prompted, it identifies what is relevant, discards distractions and acts. If a organization a banker follows makes the news, the agent assesses the significance, considers the consequences and produces analysis in the firm’s house formats within minutes instead of days.

Recent findings suggest that the platform supports a range of deployment options and is frequently installed inside clients’ own infrastructure, meaning their data stays in their environment. Client data is never used for AI model training, helping institutions protect their competitive advantage. The firm holds ISO/IEC 27001:2022 certification and has completed a SOC 2 Type II audit.

Model ML does not depend on a single AI vendor. It tests models against genuine financial tasks and assigns each job to whichever model offers the best balance of quality, speed and cost. An increasing proportion of its workload is handled by its own fine-tuned open-source models, which on those tasks cost 2% of what frontier models do, are typically five times quicker and equal or exceed frontier-level accuracy.

The new round builds on a $75m Series A led by FT Partners in November 2025, which also drew backing from Y Combinator, LocalGlobe, Latitude, 13Books Capital and QED Investors.

Model ML co-founder and CEO Chaz Englander remarked, “AI should do more than give you another answer or notification. It should understand your work and get things done.

“That means knowing what matters, doing the work in the background and bringing you something finished. We’re building a personal AI agent for every banker, consultant and investor, working 24/7 inside the systems their firm already trusts.”.

General Atlantic managing director and global head of financial services Paul Stamas said, “Model ML is purpose-built for financial and professional services at a time when these institutions are moving quickly from AI experimentation to everyday use. We see a significant opportunity for the platform to become core to how these firms operate, with customers already trusting it with increasingly complex work.

“Model ML’s pace of customer adoption shows that momentum is inflecting and reflects the team’s highly focused approach to innovation and execution.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Global Kiwi Labs, the developer behind digital asset colocation network TheHUB, has closed a $4m seed round as it looks to bring the equal-access trading architecture used by major traditional exchanges to digital asset markets.

Recent findings suggest that valor Capital Group led the round. Adderall Capital, Keyrock and Staking Facilities also invested, alongside a small number of angel backers.

Sources indicate that theHUB’s first site, which is located within the Equinix TY15 data centre in Tokyo and is now live and bringing on exchanges, trading firms and validators. The manufacturer will also use the money to add engineers to its team and move into further regions.

In a recent development, global Kiwi Labs is targeting a structural gap in digital asset trading. Traditional exchanges have worked for decades to stop any participant from paying for a quicker route to the order book, but digital asset markets never developed an equivalent layer.

As a result, the biggest players pay for proximity, while the rest of the market relies on slower and inconsistent links. A firm that spots a price change first can trade against participants still quoting the outdated price.

The company argues this affects more than high-frequency traders. When market makers cannot be confident their quotes will land on time, they widen spreads to offset the risk, which raises costs for every buyer and seller. Removing that uncertainty would allow tighter quoting and better pricing across the market.

TheHUB adapts four elements of traditional exchange infrastructure for digital assets. Each participant’s link to the central switch uses an identical length of fibre, calibrated to within 10 millimetres, so no firm gains a proximity edge to the matching engine.

The company said that as additional exchanges and infrastructure providers join, participants gain access to a wider ecosystem without having to replicate connectivity or infrastructure spending.

Founded in 2025, TheHUB describes itself as the first colocation infrastructure purpose-built for digital markets, positioned as a transaction centre where digital assets and traditional finance meet.

Valor Capital Group partner Bruno Batavia noted, “At Valor, we look for companies building the critical infrastructure that will support the next generation of financial markets. TheHUB is developing an essential technology layer that enables digital asset markets to achieve the performance standards required by global institutional participants. Jamie and his team have demonstrated an ambitious vision combined with exceptional execution, and we’re excited to support them through this next stage of growth.”.

According to recent reports, global Kiwi Labs CEO Jamie Brown noted, Traditional financial markets didn’t reach today’s levels of performance through software alone. They built specialized physical infrastructure around the markets themselves. Digital asset markets are reaching the point where they need the same foundation. We’re building TheHUB so exchanges, traders, and infrastructure providers can access that foundation as a shared network rather than rebuilding it independently.”.

Context Has a Price: Adding and Removing Context for LLM Coding Agents under Prefix Caching

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (194 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.22238v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: Coding agents repeatedly send their conversation history to a language model. Adding useful code may reduce search, while removing old tool outputs may shorten later prompts. But do these changes reduce the cost of solving a task? We study this as a measurement problem in more than 20,000 runs of open models on SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench and Loc-Bench. We account separately for uncached input, cached input and output tokens. Three findings emerge. First, in our main evidence-package experiments, retrieved code reduces read and search commands by 18--34%, but increases cost by 33--42% when cached input costs one tenth of uncached input, without a measurable improvement in resolution. Second, removing old observations can either save money or increase cost: the same approach saves 19--36% without a cache discount but increases cost by 38--116% with a tenth-price cache. Third, shorter prompts do not guarantee cheaper runs because agents may respond by taking more steps. We also find that concurrent experiments can share cached prefixes and distort cost comparisons. These results show why context-management methods should be evaluated using both token prices and the agent's subsequent behavior.

Tech Report: AWS Transit Gateway now shares resource context with firewalls for segmentation policies

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (297 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, AWS Transit Gateway now supports context sharing with security services, such as attached firewalls, allowing you to use Amazon Virtual Private Clouds (VPCs), VPC subnets, VPC security groups, and transit gateway attachments in firewall policies alongside IP addresses.
  • Transit Gateway embeds resource context in the traffic it sends to your firewall, which can enforce the right policy from the first packet.
  • Recent findings suggest that AWS Network Firewall and Palo Alto Networks Software Firewalls support policies using resource context alongside IP-based rules.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, AWS Transit Gateway now supports context sharing with security services, such as attached firewalls, allowing you to use Amazon Virtual Private Clouds (VPCs), VPC subnets, VPC security groups, and transit gateway attachments in firewall policies alongside IP addresses. Until now, attached firewalls segmented traffic by IP address, which is hard to strategy and maintain, or by resource tags, which firewalls periodically synchronize with IP addresses and can miss newly introduced workloads in between. With this feature, you can enforce segmentation based on how workloads and attachments are defined in AWS.

Transit Gateway embeds resource context in the traffic it sends to your firewall, which can enforce the right policy from the first packet. For example, you can apply threat protection to traffic between web-tier and database-tier security groups, block development VPCs from reaching production VPCs, apply a common inspection policy to traffic entering AWS through AWS Direct Connect and AWS Site-to-Site VPN attachments, or apply policies to short-lived AWS Lambda functions as soon as they send traffic, all without updating rules as IP addresses change.

Recent findings suggest that AWS Network Firewall and Palo Alto Networks Software Firewalls support policies using resource context alongside IP-based rules. To get started, create a context store in AWS Network Manager and associate your transit gateways. The context store monitors resources connected to those transit gateways and shares their context with firewalls.

In a recent development, context sharing with security services is available in all commercial AWS Regions where AWS Transit Gateway is available, except Middle East (Bahrain) and Middle East (UAE). It is also available in the AWS GovCloud (US-East) and AWS GovCloud (US-West) Regions.

To learn more, visit the AWS Transit Gateway product page and context sharing with security services documentation.

  • The marketplace extends the functionality of Portfolio Analytics, a tool more than 1,000 financial institutions currently rely on for loan-level performance insight, individualised forward-looking risk modelling, balance sheet management and compliance with the Current Expected Credit Losses standard.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

nCino, the agentic AI banking platform, has made its Loan Marketplace for participations generally available to US financial institutions.

Banks and credit unions that already use nCino Portfolio Analytics can access the upcoming product straight away within their existing nCino instance.

The marketplace extends the functionality of Portfolio Analytics, a tool more than 1,000 financial institutions currently rely on for loan-level performance insight, individualised forward-looking risk modelling, balance sheet management and compliance with the Current Expected Credit Losses standard.

Industry observers note that since each institution’s loan information is already standardised within its Portfolio Analytics environment, there is no need to recreate a loan tape in a spreadsheet or separate application. Sellers can assemble pools directly from their own portfolio data, while prospective buyers can examine a pool’s analytics, along with risk and performance details for each individual loan, before submitting an offer.

The result is a single destination where institutions can sell, purchase and oversee participations, covering everything from pre-commitment pool analysis to post-closing remittance calculation and validation.

It has been revealed that on the selling side, the platform offers guided pool building based on eligibility criteria and retention rules set by the seller. It also provides pool analytics spanning concentration, credit risk, gross yield and pricing sensitivity, as well as role-based approval controls that record who created and who signed off each listing.

Buyers, meanwhile, can review pools using loan-level risk and performance analytics, export a list of the loans involved and work through a due diligence process in which expressions of interest, letters of intent and supporting documentation are exchanged inside the marketplace.

Industry observers note that for ongoing management, a guided monthly reconciliation highlights any discrepancies and demands seller review and approval before funds are released. Owners also gain a consistent view of performance, delinquency, charge-offs, maturity and concentration for pools traded via the marketplace, as well as for sold pools brought in from other sources.

Participations have become an notable lever for balance sheet management, with institutions often mapping out purchases and sales months in advance to hit portfolio goals such as loan-to-share or loan-to-deposit ratios when fresh lending falls short. They also help firms tackle concentration risk by broadening their portfolios beyond the loans they can originate themselves. At 31 October 2026, nCino’s Portfolio Analytics customers held over $21bn in loan participations and trade substantial volumes annually. However, the supporting tools have lagged behind.

Sources indicate that according to nCino, brokers, listing boards and existing participation marketplaces typically do not hold the underlying portfolio data. As a result, buyers frequently price pools without proper visibility into the loans they contain, and post-sale servicing often depends on spreadsheets sent by email in varying formats. By linking the marketplace to each institution’s own data in Portfolio Analytics, nCino aims to introduce more transparency, automation and efficiency to a market historically driven by personal contacts, phone calls and spreadsheets.

nCino serves more than 2,700 customers globally, ranging from community banks, credit unions and independent mortgage banks to some of the world’s largest financial organisations. Its agentic platform is designed specifically for financial services and other regulated sectors, pairing AI agents with human staff to help institutions remove inefficiencies, improve decision-making and achieve better results for their customers.

Sources indicate that nCino CEO Sean Desmond remarked, “Participation trading keeps growing across the industry. Because we already hold each institution’s loan-level performance data through Portfolio Analytics, sellers and buyers can analyze a pool in detail before they commit. That data foundation is what sets nCino Loan Marketplace apart, and it gives our customers a better path to diversified, efficient and healthier balance sheets.”.

Recent findings suggest that amplify Credit Union chief lending officer JC San Pedro stated, “What stands out about the Marketplace is the combination of data and reach. We get consistent, loan-level detail on every pool, and we’re connected to a network of over one thousand financial institutions. That means we can find the right counterparties faster and evaluate opportunities with real transparency.”.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: The Fragility of Reasoning-Importance Attribution for Pruning Language Models

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (270 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.22234v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Attribution-guided pruning scores components by their causal contribution and protects the key ones, and it is increasingly applied to compress reasoning language models without destroying their chain of thought. Its reliability rests on an unexamined assumption: that reasoning importance can be faithfully measured. Across four small reasoning models, we show this measurement is fragile in three ways, each of which changes pruning decisions. First, scoring final-answer tokens, the natural choice, saturates in every chain-of-thought model we test (answer-token negative log-likelihood, NLL, of $10^{-4}$--$10^{-3}$) because the model states its answer inside its own reasoning; guiding head pruning with this target costs 27.6 and 32.2 accuracy points relative to scoring reasoning tokens on the two models we power with five seeds, while perplexity barely moves and even reverses sign at 7B. Second, causal importance is not localizable to single units: single-neuron effects sit at the measurement floor, their cross-split ranking is noise, and they cancel: a group's ablation effect disagrees in sign with the summed effects of its members in 90\% of groups. Reproducible importance emerges only at groups of $\sim 100$ neurons. Third, contrastively isolated ``reasoning-specific'' importance is not separable from generic importance, and protecting it is worse than protecting raw importance. We additionally pre-registered the hypothesis that distillation-induced concentration of importance predicts the pruning cost; it is not supported, and since our grid confounds concentration with scale, we report it as unresolved rather than reversed. The result is a short set of measurement rules: score reasoning tokens, attribute at coarse granularity, and evaluate with accuracy rather than perplexity.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The launch gives family offices, wealth owners and advisors a way to use compatible outside AI applications with their financial information.
  • The MCP server sits on top of the firm’s current API framework.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Masttro, a global platform serving as the system of record for complex wealth reporting, has rolled out a Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server alongside a fresh Developer Portal.

The launch gives family offices, wealth owners and advisors a way to use compatible outside AI applications with their financial information.

The MCP server sits on top of the firm’s current API framework. It lets eligible clients link chosen wealth data to third-party AI environments through an open interoperability standard, so they are not tied to any one AI vendor. Clients must authorise any connection, and access is read-only. It covers data such as holdings, transactions and performance, as well as the entity and ownership structures held in Masttro.

According to recent reports, this context matters most for families whose wealth spans several institutions, jurisdictions, asset classes and legal entities. Masttro does more than consolidate financial data. It also records how assets connect to ownership entities, trusts and beneficiaries, which gives AI-supported financial analysis a broader base to work from.

The launch was built around three architectural priorities. The first is richer context: compatible applications can draw on selected holdings, transactions, performance figures and ownership links, within the limits of the authenticated user’s permissions.

Recent findings suggest that the second is client control. MCP access is switched off by default and only works once a client explicitly activates and authorises it. Client administrators decide who has access and can withdraw permissions or turn off connectivity entirely. Because the server is read-only, outside applications cannot change Masttro records, start transactions or write data back.

The third is defined security boundaries. Masttro’s existing authentication, authorisation and security controls apply to all data accessed through MCP. After data reaches an authorised AI environment, the client’s chosen provider is responsible for how it is processed, stored, retained and protected.

It has been revealed that the MCP offering sits alongside Masttro Intelligence, the firm’s own model-agnostic AI environment. Masttro Intelligence handles advanced analysis, document processing and operational efficiency. It keeps AI orchestration, permissions and governance inside Masttro, so clients do not need to send their underlying wealth data to outside AI tools. Clients can therefore choose between governed in-platform AI and optional, client-authorised links to external applications.

The Developer Portal gives client technical teams and developers API and MCP documentation, authentication guidance, setup instructions and worked integration examples.

Masttro co-founder Domingo Viesca said, “As AI models continue to evolve, the strategic value lies not in any individual model, but in the quality, context, and governance of the information they can access.

In a recent development, “Masttro provides that foundation for complex wealth. Our MCP Server gives clients the flexibility to authorize external AI tools when appropriate, while maintaining control over access to their information. Masttro Intelligence remains our integrated environment for delivering advanced AI capabilities within our own security and governance framework.”.

Fine-Grained Japanese Clinical Named Entity Recognition: A Controlled Comparison of BERT and Open-Weight Large Language Models

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (247 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.22219v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Background: Generative large language models (LLMs) offer an alternative to encoder-based clinical named entity recognition (NER), but their performance on fine-grained Japanese extraction tasks and sensitivity to generation settings remain uncertain. Methods: We compared two fine-tuned BERT-CRF baselines with nine open-weight LLMs on iCorpus, which defines 113 entity categories. The evaluation used 433 sentences from 36 test documents; 1,672 sentences were used for training. LLMs were evaluated using zero-shot prompting with and without JSON Schema constraints and three-seed QLoRA fine-tuning. Fine-tuned models were assessed under different output-token limits, including 900 and larger model-specific limits of 2,600 or 4,096 tokens. Performance was measured using sentence-level label-surface matching with relaxed and exact-surface F1. Results: The highest zero-shot relaxed F1 was 0.337, compared with 0.836-0.841 for the BERT baselines. At the larger output limits, all eight fine-tuned LLMs with at least 13B total parameters exceeded both BERT baselines (relaxed F1, 0.882-0.914; exact-surface F1, 0.840-0.880). Across three-seed means, increasing the output limit improved relaxed F1 by 0.052-0.085, alongside higher recall and fewer length-limited outputs. JSON Schema constraints changed relaxed F1 by -0.014 to +0.008 among seven models outside the two reasoning-oriented configurations, while medical-general model pairs showed no consistent advantage for medical specialization. Conclusions: On this historical Japanese case-report benchmark, task-specific fine-tuning combined with adequate generation capacity was associated with stronger LLM extraction performance. Output-token limits materially affected comparisons with BERT, whereas enforcing output structure alone did not overcome low zero-shot accuracy.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Personal cyber cover has become a fixture of US homeowners policies, and AI-powered fraud is now testing whether its pricing and terms can hold.

Upcoming analysis from ZestyAI, a provider of a risk decision platform for property and casualty insurers, shows carriers are adding restrictions and reconsidering pricing after ten years of steady growth in the product.

The report, titled Cyber Moves Into the Home, examines US homeowners insurance regulatory filings between 2016 and 2026, including filings for standalone personal cyber products.

It has been revealed that zestyAI compiled the findings using ZORRO Discover, its competitive intelligence platform. The study traces how the cover grew from a specialist add-on into a widely offered endorsement protecting against six main threats: cyber attacks, cyber extortion, online fraud, data breaches, cyberbullying and identity recovery.

Recent filings point to a change in strategy. Rather than lifting rates on current policies, insurers are launching new products with higher prices and amended terms. War and cyber-war exclusions show this shift most clearly.

Sources indicate that these clauses appeared in only 5% of personal cyber programmes before 2023 but feature in 71% in 2026, the first broad tightening after seven years of expansion. State regulators have reacted inconsistently. Texas and Virginia approved the exclusions while Upcoming York and North Carolina turned them down, leaving policyholders with different protection depending on where they live.

It has been revealed that the threat is growing rapidly. FBI figures referenced in the study put reported US cybercrime losses at $20.9bn in 2025, a 26% rise on the previous year. Federal Trade Commission data shows imposter fraud losses hit $3.5bn, close to triple the 2020 figure, as voice cloning and other AI tools make impersonation schemes more convincing.

It has been revealed that pricing, however, has stayed almost flat for eight years. A typical yearly premium sits at about $55, and entry-level charges usually fall between $30 and $75. That band has held since 2018, even though insurers have widened the endorsement and raised maximum limits from $50,000 at launch to as much as $2m.

The report also finds that personal cyber cover reached uniformity more swiftly than any modern personal-lines product. Most programmes rely on common policy forms supported by reinsurers rather than wording each carrier builds alone. This allowed rapid rollout, but it also means amendments to wording and exclusions tend to move through the market in waves.

It has been revealed that carriers are also writing more precise terms for social-engineering fraud, where criminals pose as trusted people or organisations to trick victims into sending money. Existing online-fraud clauses usually cover these losses, but newer policies increasingly define and price them as a separate risk.

It has been revealed that zestyAI founder and CEO Attila Toth remarked, “Personal cyber went from a niche endorsement to a standard part of the homeowners policy in under a decade, at a price that has barely moved since 2018. What is happening now is AI is changing the risk itself faster than any product cycle this industry has experienced before.

“We are already seeing carriers define social engineering as its own coverage, raise limits, and narrow terms around systemic events. The regulatory filings provide an early indication of how the industry is responding to these emerging threats.”.

  • Recent findings suggest that you can use resource optimization on EKS Auto Mode clusters running Kubernetes 1.36 or later in the following AWS Regions: US East (N.

It has been revealed that amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) introduces resource optimization for EKS Auto Mode, a fresh capability that rightsizes the CPU and memory requests of running Pods based on their actual usage. CPU and memory requests are often set at deploy time and rarely revisited, and Auto Mode provisions EC2 instances to fit them. Rightsizing lets Auto Mode run the same Deployments and StatefulSets on fewer or smaller instances, without hand tuning and at no additional charge.

It has been revealed that turn on resource optimization by creating a ClusterResourceOptimizationPolicy in your EKS cluster, review its recommendations in the default Recommend mode, and switch to Apply mode when you're ready to resize running Pods in place, without recreating them. For example, a platform team running Java services under Argo CD can rightsize every application namespace without editing templates or creating GitOps drift, while resource optimization keeps memory above each Java heap and raises memory after an out-of-memory kill. It doesn't change the CPU or memory that a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler or KEDA scales on, and you can exclude workloads that the Vertical Pod Autoscaler already manages.

Recent findings suggest that you can use resource optimization on EKS Auto Mode clusters running Kubernetes 1.36 or later in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Ireland), Asia Pacific (Seoul), and Asia Pacific (Tokyo).

To learn more, see Rightsize workloads with resource optimization in the Amazon EKS User Guide and the EKS Auto Mode product page.

RAG in a Trenchcoat: When Minimal Memory Is Enough for Agentic Systems, and When It Isn't

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (294 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.22179v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: Agentic memory research has accumulated extraction, supersession, reflection, and graph synthesis on top of retrieval-augmented generation. However, we found that almost none of those primitives earn their cost in our tested memory benchmarks: we show this with BRIDGE, a deliberately minimal RAG memory with chained observation notes, hybrid BM25 with cosine retrieval, and chronological rendering, which reaches parity within bootstrap CI with the prior SOTA on LongMemEval-S and BEAM, and beats the best memory baseline on EverMemBench by 5.7-6.3 points at matched reader. It runs at ~5-7K reader-prompt tokens per query, using a single LLM call for each ingestion or query. We argue that this parity is itself the result: standard benchmarks score what memory retrieves, not what memory enables when the agent acts. To test the latter, we introduce five adversarial probes (Rule Application +-, Pattern Induction Style / Procedural, Dynamic Multiturn) judged at generation time by a cross vendor verification chain, where each query can only be solved by applying a remembered rule or pattern it never mentions. Across 5 probes x 20 scenarios, no architecture wins universally: atomic fact extractors (LangMem) win rule application, while BRIDGE's block-summary memory wins pattern induction. This result holds across four domains, three graders, and three reader families. Each design fails where the other wins, for reasons a recall benchmark cannot see: atomic-fact extractors discard the form a demonstrated pattern takes, while block-summary memory retrieves the rule but the reader does not act on it, a gap that presenting the rule more prominently largely closes. What separates memory designs is not what they retrieve but what they enable an agent to do, and that is what agentic memory should be evaluated on.

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.22178v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Precipitation nowcasting models suffer from errors in intensity, location, and spatial structure. Addressing these errors by retraining nowcaster backbones can be computationally expensive and requires architecture-specific modifications. To overcome these limitations, we propose CorrectCast, a decoupled residual correction framework that refines completed nowcasts while keeping the base nowcaster frozen. By operating on predicted precipitation fields, CorrectCast requires training only a lightweight corrector, reducing computational overhead while providing a unified correction interface across different nowcasting models. Conditioned on the base nowcast and historical quantitative precipitation estimation (QPE) and precipitable water vapor (PWV) observations, the corrector selects multimodal context and employs scale-aware modulation to estimate residual corrections. On the Mississippi River Basin (MRB) and contiguous United States (CONUS) datasets, CorrectCast improves six base nowcasters spanning extrapolation-based, deterministic, and generative approaches, with absolute gains in mean CSI averaging 0.0233 and 0.0290 across the six models, respectively.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, torchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a upcoming backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TorchNeuron provides a upcoming native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels natively support it, making it easier than ever to run models on Trainium and to share them on the HF hub.

In a recent development, torchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a upcoming backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP. Read the Pytorch blog to learn more about TorchNeuron.

In a recent development, starting Oct. 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta. Researchers and developers will be able to install it with pip install torch-neuronx.

To date, the Hugging Face experience on AWS Trainium and Inferentia — AI chips designed respectively for cost-effective training and inference at scale — has been delivered through optimum-neuron. This library relies on the torch-neuronx package, which is based on PyTorch XLA. It was the natural choice at the time, but it meant thinking like a compiler: lazy tensors instead of eager execution, static shapes only, a recompilation for every graph break. Optimum Neuron existed to hide that complexity, and maintained custom code (modeling classes, trainers, etc) to do so.

Industry observers note that torchNeuron changes this. It integrates directly into PyTorch and exposes neuron as a native device, with eager execution, PyTorch's own distributed primitives (DTensor, FSDP2) and torch.compile.

For the Hugging Face libraries, Trainium becomes a device like any other: Transformers, Diffusers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL run on it directly, with the same classes and scripts you would use on any other accelerator. From now on, we recommend that Neuron people use these libraries directly instead of going through Optimum Neuron.

It has been revealed that text generation is now natively supported in Transformers for a wide range of models. With TorchNeuron, 89% of the top 100 most-used text-generation model architectures are supported out of the box, compared to 46% with Optimum Neuron v0.4.5. You just need to pass the device_map=neuron argument in your code and your model will be moved to the Neuron devices.

Sources indicate that the following is an example of text-generation with tensor parallelism, which will enable to fully benefit from your Neuron instance. Note that it uses a static cache for generation as this is strongly recommended with Neuron to prevent frequent recompilations.

Recent findings suggest that now that Neuron is a native PyTorch device, training on Trainium uses the same Hugging Face libraries as any other accelerator: Transformers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL. You no longer need a dedicated trainer or a Neuron-specific fork of the model code. A standard TRL fine-tuning script runs on a Trainium instance with only a few Neuron-specific settings.

Here is a supervised fine-tuning script built on TRL's SFTTrainer. If you have fine-tuned a model with TRL on GPUs before, it should look familiar.

Parallelism is handled natively by Transformers. You put a DistributedConfig with the tensor-parallel (TP) and FSDP sizes in model_init_kwargs, SFTTrainer passes it to from_pretrained, and the model is sharded as its weights are loaded. The Trainer sees that the model is already distributed and does not wrap it again. You don't need an --fsdp flag or an Accelerate FSDP config.

According to recent reports, nothing in the script is tied to Trainium: the same code runs on any hardware. A few things are worth knowing when you run it on Trainium:.

Industry observers note that the command below introduces training with torchrun, which starts one process per NeuronCore. TP_SIZE and FSDP_SIZE set the parallelism layout, and their product is the number of processes: here 4 x 8 = 32, matching --nproc_per_node. The 32 processes form a 4 x 8 grid. Tensor parallelism splits each layer across the 4 cores of a TP group, and FSDP shards the parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the 8 TP groups.

We ran it on 8 Trainium2 chips (32 NeuronCores), which is half a trn2.48xlarge instance.

Training runs to completion, and trainer.save_model writes a standard Transformers checkpoint. Nothing in it is tied to Neuron: you can push it to the Hugging Face Hub as is and load it on any other hardware.

According to recent reports, many pipelines from the Diffusers library are compatible with TorchNeuron in eager and compiled mode. FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.2, Qwen-Image, Qwen-Image-2.1 and H3 are also compatible with tensor parallelism to make the most of your Neuron devices. The following is an example showing how you can use TP:.

You can run this piece of code with: NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG=2 torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 run.py.

Sources indicate that more and more pipleines will be compatible with TP. If a pipeline you like is not, you can also add support for it following this guide.

Sources indicate that make sure to check out the kernels from the Neuron team as more and more Neuron kernels will become available on the Hub to speed up your models. Neuron kernels can be written using the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI), which gives lower control to optimize operations. This way, owners can run their own custom operations and share them on the hub.

You can use for example this kernel to speed up your vision transformers with up to a x2.4 speedup on Trainium!

In a recent development, AWS Transform now supports AWS Outposts as a migration target. You can migrate workloads onto your Outposts from on-premises environments, another Outpost, or a different Availability Zone or Region. AWS Transform is a collaborative enterprise IT transformation service powered by agentic AI that accelerates cloud migration, application modernization, and continuous tech debt reduction. Run your migration with AI agents in AWS Transform for migrations, or use AWS Transform MGN, the rehost engine within AWS Transform, directly from its console.

If you run workloads on Outposts for low latency, local data processing, or data residency, migrating them has meant manual effort or legacy tooling, often with a detour through the Region and an AMI copy. Now you choose subnets on the Outpost for your migration, and AWS Transform continuously replicates your source servers at the block level, directly from your source environment to the Outpost. You launch test instances before cutover and cut over with minimal downtime.

Sources indicate that migration to Outposts is available in all AWS Transform for migrations target Regions and AWS Transform MGN Regions and requires Amazon EBS on the Outpost. If your Outpost has Amazon S3 on Outposts, you can keep snapshots on the Outpost for data residency or store them in the parent Region. Without it, snapshots are stored in the parent Region.

To get started, see the AWS Transform documentation or visit the AWS Transform product page.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (271 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

arXiv:2611.22177v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) trading agents are tested on news, but news reaches stock prices within minutes, and a benchmark that replays headlines at their publication time finds no alpha in trading on them. Money can then remain in two places, before news whose date is known, such as earnings announcements, and after bad news, if the market's fall went too far. However, studies of LLMs and earnings read documents published with or after the announcement, and studies of reversal sort monthly portfolios, so neither tells whether an agent can trade these moments after costs. In this paper, we test LLM agents at both moments on the same look-ahead-free benchmark, before 598 earnings announcements and after 409 bad-news drops of large US stocks. Every input is cut at the decision close, staged agents are compared with single calls, simple rules and a logistic regression, and every decision is made with and without the stock's name. Across five models from four vendors, no agent beat the simple bets. Before earnings, the agents mostly bought and earned what buying before every announcement earned, and after bad news, a Gemini-based agent called almost every fall an overreaction while no agent picked better dips than buying them all. The only gains came from what the models had memorized in training. Given only the ticker and the dates, a GPT-based model called the direction of 59.2% of the announcements before its training cutoff and 53.3% after it. Agent builders should therefore compare an event agent with the simple bet and test it blind after the training cutoff.

MPS in PyTorch 2.15

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1362 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15!
  • Sources indicate that A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face.
  • If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and latest Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.

Sources indicate that A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors.

If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.

You'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why.

To try the release candidate in a separate environment:.

FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds torch.float8_e4m3fn tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.

Recent findings suggest that you can multiply these tensors with F.scaled_mm, which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:.

Sources indicate that every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each new token goes through the model as a single row, so the major matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers.

In a recent development, MPS has had GEMV kernels for torch.mm since 2.14, but F.linear still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to F.linear, so the common [1, 1, hidden_size] decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.

A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation.

In 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The newly introduced Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well.

For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:.

The decoding kernel shows up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with torch.compile, MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second:.

Industry observers note that working with complex tensors gets easier. complex64 LU factorization, LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:.

In a recent development, small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: QR uses blocked updates, and triangular solves turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication.

Gated DeltaNet workloads get a dedicated fast path for batches of 16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems with at least eight right-hand sides.

Industry observers note that SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles very small singular values, very large or very small input magnitudes and basis completion with full_matrices=True, which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable.

Audio models, video decoders and training loops have their own expensive operations. This release gives several of them newly introduced paths through Metal:.

Token sampling gets faster in 2.15 as well. softmax and log_softmax now run on dedicated Metal kernels, and large vocabularies benefit the most: an FP32 softmax over a [1, 128256] row of logits drops from 57 µs to 7 µs, about 8× faster than the MPSGraph version. The speedup holds across other common vocabulary sizes:.

Sources indicate that one of the most striking results in this release comes from the constant-padding change. The VAE decode in Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers makes 8,764 padding calls over a full 28-tile decode. With padding on Metal, peak driver memory drops from about 270 GiB to 8 GiB:.

Industry observers note that you can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. torch.mps.Stream and the torch.mps.stream context manager provide the interface, and Tensor.record_stream lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream.

Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result:.

Industry observers note that several more operations now run on MPS: torch.frexp, torch.logspace, torch.take and Tensor.put_, torch.heaviside, torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l and unsigned-integer comparisons. logspace doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element.

Attention gets a correctness fix too: the MPS math implementation of scaled dot-product attention now handles batch and head broadcasting correctly.

Recent findings suggest that work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on main and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release.

Once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 commits the command buffer every 16 kernels, so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context:.

According to recent reports, scaled dot-product attention is dropping MPSGraph completely: every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms.

It has been revealed that the move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm forward and backward are in progress, while MSE loss (up to 12× faster on small inputs), std_mean and var_mean (up to 4× faster) and bincount have already landed. bincount is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond.

Bundled shaders will build for Metal 3.1 by default, with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks libtorch_cpu.dylib by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication.

PyTorch 2.15 brings FP8 to the Mac, faster LLM decoding for dense and MoE models, more linear algebra on the GPU and a long list of operations moved from MPSGraph to dedicated Metal kernels. Give the release candidate a try!

A big thank you to Nikita Shulga, Kurt Mohler and Aaron Gokaslan for reviewing much of this work, and to everyone who contributed to MPS in this release.

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.22174v1 Announce Type: fresh Abstract: General-purpose behavior models increasingly internalize broad procedural knowledge during training, making their adaptation to new goals and skill interfaces less a problem of learning entirely new behaviors than of reconfiguring existing competence. We study this capability as reconfigurability, the ability to realize new behaviors by cost-efficiently restructuring existing components and relations under sparse governing information, where task specifications provide high-level goals and procedure specifications expose a limited set of reusable factors, leaving the concrete bindings and compositions required for execution underdetermined. We propose RecPo, a framework that represents skills task-agnostically through multiple procedure views and materializes executable skill sequences by composing stored transitions to realize task-specific changes. RecPo maintains a procedure knowledge base of skill-induced transitions, with each view exposing a reusable factor and preserving local skill connectivity. At deployment, it interprets task specifications through the same views and resolves the resulting compositional queries over the stored relations to bind skills for execution. On long-horizon tasks in an extended Franka Kitchen benchmark, RecPo achieves 91.9% ordered completion with 1.0 ms of task inference per episode across varying procedure support and task-record sparsity. Real-robot studies further demonstrate adaptation through local memory edits without task-specific retraining.

Sources indicate that amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference now supports NVIDIA Dynamo. You can now serve models that are too large for a single instance, and keep token generation fast when prompts are long. You don't have to build or operate distributed serving infrastructure yourself. HyperPod manages Dynamo for you through the Inference Operator add-on.

In a recent development, as models grow, two problems limit inference. A large model can need more GPU memory than one instance has. Long prompts also slow token generation, because the prefill and decode stages compete for the same GPUs. Until now, customers had to build and run their own distributed serving stack to work around both.

With Dynamo on HyperPod, you can run a single model across multiple nodes. You can also split prefill and decode into separate GPU pools that scale independently, so a long prompt no longer stalls token generation for other requests. KV-aware routing sends each request to a worker that already holds the relevant cached context. This cuts recomputation and raises throughput. HyperPod runs the underlying infrastructure: EFA networking, GPU capacity management, node replacement, endpoint registration, autoscaling, and observability. Your team can spend its time on the models instead.

Industry observers note that to get started, bring your existing Dynamo manifests if you want full control. You can also use a simplified configuration that HyperPod translates into the underlying infrastructure.

Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference with NVIDIA Dynamo support is available in US East (N. Virginia, Ohio), US West (N. California, Oregon), Europe (Frankfurt, Stockholm, Ireland, London, Spain), Asia Pacific (Mumbai, Hyderabad, Singapore, Sydney, Jakarta, Melbourne, Tokyo), and South America (São Paulo). To learn more, see the Amazon SageMaker HyperPod documentation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The global economy has proved more resilient than many expected this year, but Italy is increasingly being left behind, according to the latest November 2026 brief from Italian consultancy and economic research firm Prometeia.

In its analysis of Italy’s position in the global economy, Prometeia found that worldwide growth has weathered both the energy shock and the rise in inflation. The main driver has been the race to invest in artificial intelligence, which is boosting business investment in the US and lifting exports across Asia. As a result, Prometeia has raised its 2026 global GDP forecast to 3%, while its projection for trade growth has climbed to 5%.

Prometeia expects major monetary authorities to keep tightening, with a further 25bp rate rise anticipated in December from both the US Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank. Europe, however, continues to sit on the sidelines of the AI-driven upswing, with regional growth expected to hover around 1.3%.

According to recent reports, italy stands out for the wrong reasons. According to Prometeia, Italian GDP flatlined in the third quarter, recording 0% growth quarter on quarter and bringing an end to four straight quarters of expansion. The firm has trimmed its 2026 growth forecast for the country to 0.8%, down from 0.9%.

Recent findings suggest that prometeia argues that the inflationary shock is now weighing directly on economic activity. The outlook for next year is weaker still, with growth projected to slow to 0.6% in 2027. A key factor is the fading impact of investments under the National Recovery and Resilience Proposal (NRRP), which have supported activity in recent years. The 2027 Budget Law is expected to offset this only in part.

Industry observers note that inflation is the other major pressure point. Prometeia reports that Italian consumer price inflation jumped to 5.4% in October, up from 4.2% in September. The surge was driven largely by regulated electricity tariffs and the cost of unprocessed food. Core inflation, which strips out more volatile components, rose more modestly to 2.0%.

It has been revealed that the firm expects headline inflation to peak at around 5.9% around the turn of the year before easing as energy prices soften. On an annual basis, Prometeia forecasts inflation will average 3.4% in 2026 and 2.7% in 2027.

Breaking: Readie: Low-Latency Code Sandboxes for AI Agents

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (208 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.22171v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: From quantitative research to personal assistance, AI agents act by iteratively generating and executing code. To decouple the agent harness from code execution, many agents offload execution to dedicated systems called code sandboxes. However, existing code sandboxes suffer from slow startup. Whether they rely on custom snapshots or a single fat image, the root cause is the same: it is hard to build a compact, pre-warmed snapshot that can be shared across diverse agent-generated code while covering nearly all the artifacts (e.g., packages, datasets) it requires. In this work, we propose learned startup snapshots for low-latency code sandboxes. Our insight is that while it is hard for a single snapshot to be both compact and cover most workloads, a set of snapshots can achieve both. Each snapshot is small, initializes rapidly, and covers a fraction of agent-generated code; together, the set covers most of it. We learn this set from a large training workload by formulating snapshot construction as an optimization problem and solving it with an approximation algorithm. Planned on 15K public and LLM-synthesized scripts, our system, Readie, reduces startup latency by 3-22$\times$ and end-to-end runtime by 1.3-3.3$\times$ compared to existing approaches at the same storage budget.

We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback.

Sources indicate that local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this newly introduced generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task.

A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0.

Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps.

Support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports:.

Language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work.
