AWS now enables agentic coding harnesses to open the latest AWS sign-up experience for developers who don't have an AWS account yet. Previously, developers working in agentic coding environments like Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor had to manually navigate to aws.amazon.com, sign up for an AWS account and configure credentials before deploying workloads, interrupting the developer's experience. Now, developers can go from an idea to deploying a running application by the browser automatically opening, completing sign up and returning short-lived credentials to the harness. When developers sign up for AWS from their coding agent, they start with the new AWS experience. Their first project comes set up with a home Region, IAM role manager, and short-term credentials that refresh automatically, so the agent can start deploying right away. To try the new experience, configure the AWS Agent Toolkit in your agentic coding harness using the AWS MCP server setup guide or install the AWS Agent Toolkit plugin. On first authentication, you'll be prompted to open a browser directly to the AWS sign-up page. You can also initiate account creation via the AWS CLI by running aws signup (opens directly to sign-up) or aws login (opens the SignIn page with a Sign Up option). To learn more, see the AWS Agent Toolkit documentation or the AWS Account Documentation.

Not All Evidence Is Admissible: Evidence Governance for Tool-Augmented Medical Agents

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (256 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.22169v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: Tool-augmented medical agents treat whatever their tools return as evidence. We show that this default is costly: medical tools fail silently, and a frozen reasoner cannot ignore what enters its context, so many cases it would have answered correctly are flipped to wrong once tool outputs are added. We call this evidence hijacking. $\mathcal{V}$-information explains the phenomenon: the reasoner has lost the option to ignore, so a tool output can carry negative usable information, and moving the decision of what to keep outside the reasoner restores that option. The theory further indicates that part of any filtering gain comes merely from letting the reasoner see less, and only selection by content lets it see better. Building on this, we recast tool-augmented reasoning as evidence governance, which separates deciding what counts as evidence from the reasoner that answers, and propose context-independent evidence governance (CIEG), the first medical agent framework that rules, after acquisition, on whether each individual tool output may enter as evidence. Every tool output is written as a card that can be checked against the raw input; an independent checker that sees only the input and the cards decides which cards become evidence; and the reasoner answers from the admitted cards alone, with no training anywhere. On medical question answering, fundus glaucoma screening, and chest X-ray pneumonia classification, it achieves the highest accuracy among models of comparable scale, and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art tool-using agents and multi-agent systems built on the same backbone at lower cost.

What’s new in OKF v0.3: enterprise-ready knowledge, use cases, and skills

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1633 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Google

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that in June we introduced the Open Knowledge Format (OKF), an open specification that provides plain markdown and YAML to give agents the context they need.
  • According to recent reports, in production, bundles move between organizations, multiple agents edit the same corpus, and independent tools need to read a bundle the same way.
  • Sources indicate that we're also launching OKF use cases, which are community guides for using OKF alongside other industry standards, and two agent skills that let coding agents write and read OKF bundles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tech Lead, BigQuery, Engineering, Data Cloud.

The front door to AI in the workplace.

Sources indicate that in June we introduced the Open Knowledge Format (OKF), an open specification that provides plain markdown and YAML to give agents the context they need. In July, v0.2 added trust signals: provenance, trust, freshness, lifecycle, and attestation.

According to recent reports, in production, bundles move between organizations, multiple agents edit the same corpus, and independent tools need to read a bundle the same way. Released today, OKF v0.3 adds precise conformance rules, trust tiers that keep pace with agent edits, self-describing bundles with licensing, safe ways to retire and move knowledge, a stable extension model, and a clear versioning policy. However, the core idea behind OKF stays the same: type is still the only required field, and your existing bundles keep working.

Sources indicate that we're also launching OKF use cases, which are community guides for using OKF alongside other industry standards, and two agent skills that let coding agents write and read OKF bundles. Finally, to make cross-organization collaboration easier, we’re moving OKF out of the Google Cloud Platform GitHub org into a standalone organization at https://github.com/open-knowledge-format/open-knowledge-format/.

Let’s take a closer look at what’s new in OKF v0.3.

Sources indicate that v0.3 adds a formal conformance section, allowing independent producers and consumers to work together by design. The spec is self-contained and uses RFC 2119 keywords. It gives one clear answer to the questions that come up when tools from different teams and vendors read the same bundle. The full detail is in the spec, but a few themes matter for anyone building on OKF:.

In a recent development, built on standard file formats. OKF uses a small, widely supported set of standards: YAML 1.2 frontmatter, CommonMark with GFM tables and footnotes, and RFC 3339 timestamps. If your tools handle those, they handle OKF.

Recent findings suggest that OKF bundles share space with other markdown files. A .md file without a type is skipped by OKF consumers, so README.md, AGENTS.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, and SKILL.md can live inside a bundle without breaking it. Files that aren't markdown, like images or attester code, are assets that concepts can link to.

Consumers handle real-world input predictably. Bundles written by many agents can contain nulls, empty strings, single values where a list was expected, and fresh vocabulary. v0.3 specifies how a consumer reads each of these. Consumers accept these inputs without failing, while validators log warnings for malformed entries. A bundle never fails because an optional field is missing or a link is broken.

v0.2 gave every concept a trust tier: unverified, machine-confirmed, or human-reviewed. As agents take on more of the editing, v0.3 makes sure the tier always reflects the latest version of the content. Here's a typical sequence:.

A person reviews a metric definition and signs off.

A week later, an agent refines the definition.

The trust tier now reflects that the person hasn't yet reviewed the new text.

Industry observers note that in v0.3, only current verifications count. A verification is current when it happened at or after the last meaningful change to the content, recorded in generated.at:.

This concept is now machine-confirmed, not human-reviewed, until a person confirms it again. The older sign-off stays in the file as history, and a UI can show it as "reviewed before the last change.".

In a recent development, v0.3 also standardizes actor identifiers. Actors are / for tools, or : for everything else, and v0.3 adds team: next to human: and process:. Only human: earns human-reviewed, because a team name doesn't say which person actually checked the content.

According to recent reports, when an agent has access to dozens of bundles, bundle-level metadata supports progressive disclosure so it can pick the right bundle without reading every file. In v0.3, the bundle-root index.md can carry frontmatter about the bundle itself:.

In a recent development, description is written for routing. In one sentence it says what the bundle covers and when to use it.

license makes clear what you're allowed to do with knowledge you receive from someone else.

okf_version tells a consumer which rules to apply, including compatibility fallbacks for older bundles.

Tools that regenerate index.md must keep this frontmatter.

Sources indicate that knowledge evolves, and an agent that finds a deprecated concept should be able to get to its replacement. v0.3 adds superseded_by:.

Consumers that filter to current knowledge follow the pointer and return the replacement. The same mechanism handles moves and renames. Leave a short deprecated concept at the old path that points to the upcoming one, and existing links and stored references keep working.

Links in the body and path fields in frontmatter (resource, superseded_by, executor.resource, and others) now resolve the same way:.

A value with a scheme (https:) is an absolute URL.

A value that starts with / resolves from the bundle root.

Anything else resolves from the directory of the file that contains it, just like on GitHub or in any markdown editor.

For bundles marked v0.2 or earlier, or with no version, a consumer can also resolve paths from the bundle root, so existing bundles keep working.

v0.3 also makes explicit that links are not parent/child relationships. Only the directory tree defines hierarchy. A link is an untyped, directed relationship, and the text around it claims what kind ("joins with," "replaces," "depends on"). Path fields that point at concepts are edges in the bundle graph too.

The community has been extending OKF since v0.1, with typed edges, routing hints, and erasure profiles. v0.3 makes a few extension mechanisms a first-class rule:.

Extension keys are allowed at any level, including inside sources entries, verified events, executor, and attester.

A producer that edits a file must keep the keys it doesn't understand so one tool doesn't overwrite metadata added by another.

Industry observers note that future OKF versions will never define keys that start with x-. Name your keys x--, for example x-acme-owner, and they won't collide with a future spec version.

It has been revealed that v0.3 defines OKF's versioning rules. Before 1.0, minor versions may include breaking changes as long as each is documented with a consumer fallback where possible. Starting at 1.0, minor versions will be strictly additive, and released normative text will not change in place.

It has been revealed that the spec also lists what was considered and deferred: typed relationships, the full attestation runtime protocol (receipt and verdict wire formats), semantic-layer attestation, validity windows, and a refuted verification event. Until the community agrees on a form for these, extension keys are the place to experiment. We'd like your proposals.

It has been revealed that OKF keeps its core specification small and links to existing domain schemas like Avro, Protobuf, or OpenAPI instead of duplicating them. In practice, though, when your organization already has an established artifact in another standard, such as a schema, a contract, or a spec, what should the OKF concept next to it say, and how should an agent use the two together?

Starting with v0.3, we're publishing use cases: guides for using OKF with other industry standards. Each one explains:.

Where the boundary sits: what belongs in the other standard and what belongs in OKF.

How to link the two: which frontmatter and link conventions point from a concept into the other artifact.

What an agent should do with the combination.

A complete worked example you can copy.

Use cases are layered on the core spec, not part of it. A bundle that ignores them is still a conformant OKF bundle. When a convention proves itself across several use cases, it can be proposed for the core spec through the usual process.

Use cases are managed directly in GitHub. Each use case gets its own folder under usecases/ in the OKF repository, for example usecases//. The guide is a .md file in that folder, and any sample bundles or artifacts sit next to it. Use cases are reviewed, versioned, and discussed like any other change.

If you pair OKF with a standard, please send us a proposal. A rough first draft is welcome. Open a pull request that adds a folder under usecases/ with a .md file in it, and we'll refine it together in review.

v0.3 has two breaking changes, and existing v0.2 bundles stay readable:.

According to recent reports, path fields resolve relative to their file. Fallback: for bundles marked v0.2 or earlier, or with no version, consumers can resolve from the bundle root.

Only current verifications count toward the trust tier. No fallback needed, since tiers can only go down.

Everything else is a clarification or an optional addition. v0.1 fallbacks (timestamp, body # Citations) still apply.

The two skills live in the latest repository and follow the open Agent Skills format, so any agent that supports skills can load them.

okf-generate writes, updates, migrates, and validates bundles from available sources. It cites a source for each claim, records a human review only when that person confirms it, and copies attested computations from a sanctioned source instead of writing them.

Sources indicate that okf-consume answers questions from a bundle. For each concept used, it reports the trust tier, status, freshness, and attestation result, and runs attested computations only through the bundle's configured executor and attester.

To install them in Gemini CLI, run:.

The README lists the install steps for other agents.

Read the v0.3 spec. Add okf_version to your bundles, and check that your consumer computes trust tiers from current verifications only. Concerns and pull requests, including upcoming use case proposals, are welcome on GitHub.

Spec, samples, use cases, and reference implementations: https://github.com/open-knowledge-format/open-knowledge-format/.

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (272 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Long-Context Generation Is a Sampling Problem (When You Turn Up the Heat)

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (272 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.22148v1 Announce Type: fresh Abstract: Open-weight language models are widely observed to get worse the longer they generate. Often, attempts to fix this involve more training. At high temperature, The sampler, i.e. the rule that picks the next token out of the model's probabilities, decides whether long and agentic generation survives and/or thrives. We test 29 open-weight models from 1B to 122B parameters on ten established benchmarks plus needle retrieval out to one million tokens, covering SWE-bench Verified coding agents, long chain-of-thought reasoning, long-form writing, long structured output and long-context reading. Samplers that keep their pool of candidate tokens small and steady as temperature rises don't lose accuracy. Samplers that let in low-probability tokens fall apart. At temperature 2, coding agents running top-p, top-k or Top-H resolve 0 of 100 GitHub issues, while the same agents running top-nsigma resolve 46 to 62 and win every problem the two samplers disagree on, on three Qwen3.5 models. Over all benchmarks top-nsigma keeps a median 100% of its temperature-1 score where top-p keeps 26%. Counting how many tokens each sampler lets through explains why. In one Llama-3.1-8B story, going from temperature 1 to 2 grows top-p's pool from 4 tokens to 51,845 while top-nsigma stays at 3. Across 133 combinations of sampler setting and temperature, the typical pool size predicts judged quality (Spearman correlation of -0.77), and when we pick the pool at temperature 1 and only apply temperature afterwards, Top-H, min-p and p-less stop collapsing. At the default temperature of 1 most samplers perform about the same, We release all code and data to the public.

  • According to recent reports, when you choose Stop next to an idle instance recommendation, a confirmation reveals the instance, its account and Region, what the instance loses when it stops, such as instance store data and data in memory, and what continues to bill, such as EBS volumes and Elastic IP addresses.

According to recent reports, AWS Cost Optimization Hub now lets you stop idle Amazon EC2 instances directly from your recommendations. Cost Optimization Hub consolidates and prioritizes cost optimization recommendations across your AWS accounts and Regions, including idle resources. Previously, stopping an idle instance required you to leave Cost Optimization Hub and identify the specific instance in the Amazon EC2 console. Now you can stop it from the Savings opportunities page in Cost Optimization Hub.

According to recent reports, when you choose Stop next to an idle instance recommendation, a confirmation reveals the instance, its account and Region, what the instance loses when it stops, such as instance store data and data in memory, and what continues to bill, such as EBS volumes and Elastic IP addresses. Stopping does not terminate the instance or delete its EBS volumes, and you can start it again from the EC2 console. Stop needs no separate setup and uses your existing permissions. To receive idle resource recommendations, turn on Cost Optimization Hub and AWS Compute Optimizer.

This feature is available at no additional charge in all AWS Regions except the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions and the China Regions.

To get started, open Cost Optimization Hub in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console and go to Savings opportunities. To learn more, see the Cost Optimization Hub product page and user guide.

Industry News: Hugging Face ❤️ TorchTPU: TPUs, Natively

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (845 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX.
  • TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit.
  • Industry observers note that TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX. With TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. It opens up native support of TPU in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels run natively on TPU. Pick a model from the Hub, send it to "tpu", and you're done.

TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit. TPUs are Google's own AI accelerators. They are chips built for one job: the matrix math that neural networks spend most of their time on. Google has been designing them for about ten years, and uses them to train and serve its own models, including Gemini.

Industry observers note that TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips. They shine when you need a lot of compute, for training or for serving at scale.

The catch has always been software. The TPU stack grew up around TensorFlow and JAX, and PyTorch users had to work harder to get in.

Until now, running PyTorch on TPUs meant going through PyTorch/XLA (torch_xla). It worked, but it had its quirks. Tensors were lazy (the tensors, not you), so your code didn't always run when you thought it did. Small changes could trigger graph recompilations, and debugging was hard to reason about.

In a recent development, to make life easier, we built Optimum TPU. It gave Hugging Face models inference and training support on TPUs. Now that TorchTPU brings native support, Optimum TPU is not required anymore to run Hugging Face models with Transformers and Diffusers.

TorchTPU adds TPU as a new backend to PyTorch. You write regular PyTorch code. It comes with Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a torch.compile integration for when you want more speed. Installing it on a TPU VM takes one command:.

It has been revealed that the extra index gives you the CPU build of torch. Without it, pip pulls the much bigger CUDA build, which you don't need on a TPU.

Transformers v5 was built around one idea: be the source of truth for model definitions, so they can run anywhere. "Anywhere" now includes TPUs. To load a model on a TPU, pass device_map="tpu". That's it.

It has been revealed that the model runs in eager mode by default. You can also use torch.compile for better performance, or run it in a distributed setup.

TPU is now a first-class device in Diffusers. For prototyping or debugging, eager mode only needs pipe.to("tpu"). For deployment, compiled mode adds one compile call. Your pipelines and code stay the same, and there's no TPU fork to maintain.

The first call compiles, and every call after that with the same image size reuses the graph.

Models too massive for one chip? Pass a TensorParallelConfig to from_pretrained and the transformer is sharded across chips as it loads, so the full model never has to fit in one place. Many popular pipelines support it out of the box, and the ones that don't are just a tp_plan away. The Diffusers TPU guide has the full recipe.

Here are some examples run on a Cloud TPU v6e-4:.

TP=4 (each model split across four chips) · bf16 · batch 1.

The Kernels Hub has ready-to-use TPU kernels. Load one with the Kernels library and give your model a speed boost.

TPU kernels are written in Pallas, which gives you low-level control over the hardware. You can also bring in kernels from the Tokamax library. Here is a ragged-dot kernel from Tokamax plugged into a Mixture-of-Experts model:.

In a recent development, the bigger the batch, the bigger the win. At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B-A4B.

Recent findings suggest that decode throughput on a TPU v6e-8, Hub kernel vs. the default implementation.

It has been revealed that we're continuously improving TPU support in transformers by running the library test suite. We are working to add a nightly CI on TPU and make the results available in the (transformers dashboard)[https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard].

According to recent reports, the Transformers CI dashboard, with TPU results next to other accelerators. Work in progress!

It's not all green yet, and we're fine with that. Of the tests that run on TPU, 96.5% pass. Every failure we find becomes a small repro script and an issue on the TorchTPU repo. So far we have reported 34 issues, and 19 are already fixed. Running on TPU also caught a few bugs in Transformers itself, like in StaticCache and the Qwen3 tensor-parallel plans. We fixed those upstream.

If something breaks on TPU, we want to find out before you do.

In a recent development, TPUs are no longer a side quest for PyTorch users. Install TorchTPU, grab a model from the Hub, and send it to "tpu".

We can't wait to see what you build 🤗. If you hit a problem, open an issue and tell us about it.

Big Brains, Tiny Board: Pupavision, an Agentic Physical AI Instrument for Monitoring Drosophila Pupariation and Lifecycle Transitions

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (297 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.22136v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many biology experiments are limited by the availability and ease of use of instruments that monitor and record them. For example, the timing of pupariation in the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster, a widely used model organism, can provide biologically relevant information about growth regulation and is often recorded manually. Here, we present Pupavision, a small physical AI instrument built from a single-board Linux computer and a day/night camera for roughly 45 to 75 US dollars in parts. The key idea is that a frontier coding agent runs its agentic harness directly on the tiny board. The model thinks in the cloud, but the agent works on the device. The agent assists image capture, writes code to repair errors, and checks the experiment every day to keep raw data capture reliable. If recording stops, the researcher gets a ping on their mobile phone. A simple deterministic capture service records one image every ten minutes and never depends on the agent. We report a 26-day pilot in a fly incubator (about 3,580 frames), including eleven days in which the agent was logged out and capture continued, and a 51-hour outage whose cause led to the layered design. A researcher-in-the-loop workflow then produces per-vial pupariation curves by tracing selected pupae backward in time from a late reference frame. Future work will validate the assay for lifecycle tracking accuracy against expert-labeled data and expand real-time computer vision analysis. Pupavision offers a blueprint for do-it-yourself agentic instruments that put frontier intelligence on a tiny board, with deterministic code underneath. We present this as an early case study from a pilot lab deployment and contribute lessons learned toward a future where scientific domain experts are empowered by DIY agentic hardware.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While global M&A lost momentum in the third quarter of 2026, Asia Pacific told a very different story. According to fresh analysis from LSEG Data & Analytics, deal value involving the region stayed broadly flat at $271.1bn in Q3, a 25% rise on the same period last year. Deals targeting Asia Pacific companies performed even better, climbing 8% quarter-on-quarter and 35% year-on-year.

Industry observers note that the headline figures mask an key shift, however. LSEG Data & Analytics notes that deal volumes are falling, suggesting the region’s resilience reflects more disciplined, selective dealmaking rather than broad-based growth.

China remained the dominant force. LSEG data shows declared deal value in the country rose 33.3% from Q2, taking its year-to-date total to $249.8bn, or 40.8% of Asia Pacific-targeted activity. Large recapitalisations at major financial institutions bolstered the numbers, technology became China’s biggest target sector, and private equity-backed deals reached a five-year high of $59.6bn, more than twice last year’s level.

Recent findings suggest that australia staged a dramatic recovery. Target M&A reached $64.7bn in Q3, up 116.7% on the previous quarter, lifting the year-to-date figure to $108.6bn, a 129.8% annual increase. Appetite for mining, resources and infrastructure assets, fuelled by interest in critical minerals and the energy transition, drove the surge.

Recent findings suggest that india’s activity was shaped by domestic consolidation, restructuring and overseas ambitions. Target M&A slipped 2.8% to $88.4bn year-to-date, though deals with any Indian involvement edged up 1.3% to $110.3bn. Outbound M&A jumped 24.1% to $21bn as Indian corporates continued to expand abroad.

Singapore cemented its role as a regional investment hub. LSEG Data & Analytics reports any-involvement activity nearly doubled, rising 98.2% to $104.3bn, while target M&A grew 88.5% to $39.2bn, its strongest first nine months in five years. Outbound deals hit a record $46.3bn, and high technology made up almost 46% of Singapore-related activity.

Recent findings suggest that strength was spread across deal sizes. In Asia Pacific excluding Japan, transactions under $1bn rose 16.4% by value and 16.3% by count year-on-year. Mega deals of $5bn or more grew 28% over the first nine months, with Q3 activity in that bracket up 45.5% on Q2.

Technology was the leading target sector, reaching $164.1bn, up 97.2% year-on-year and representing 21.7% of regional activity, the second-highest total since LSEG records began in 1980. Investment in AI, data centres and digital infrastructure powered much of this, with transactions involving Anthropic, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, STT GDC and DayOne Data Centers. Yet materials, financials, industrials and energy & power together accounted for over half of all activity.

Private equity also shone. Sponsor-backed M&A reached $131.4bn over nine months, up 101.4% from $65.2bn, with deal count up 62.2%. Q3 value eased 2.9% to $46.6bn and deal count fell 23%, though this followed a Q2 that was the strongest quarter since Q4 2021. Valuations, financing conditions and geopolitics continue to temper deployment.

It has been revealed that looking ahead, LSEG Data & Analytics concludes that investors are becoming more disciplined but not less active. For dealmakers, success will depend on understanding where each market’s local drivers meet the region’s shared pull towards AI, digital infrastructure and strategic resources.

CDON (Sweden): As the largest e-commerce marketplace in the Nordics, CDON modernized its backend and data infrastructure on Google Cloud. Its analytics pipelines run on Google BigQuery, dbt, and Google Cloud Storage, utilizing Python and FastAPI to ingest massive volumes of retail marketplace data. CDON democratizes real-time business reporting across brands and lays the groundwork for predictive personalization and generative AI workloads.

Chalkie.ai (UK):  A fast-growing education technology platform, Chalkie.ai uses Gemini's advanced reasoning capabilities to transform lesson planning for over 500,000 educators. By exporting directly to Google Slides Google Slides, teachers can instantly generate curriculum-aligned presentations and materials directly within their instructional tools while maintaining strict student data privacy standards.

Finova (UK): A leader in UK lending and savings software, has released the UK’s first whole-of-market AI mortgage application agent, built on Google Cloud and Gemini. By deploying Gemini’s advanced reasoning to automate complex mortgage applications across multiple lender portals, Finova removes manual data entry bottlenecks and reduces errors. This saves mortgage brokers at least 30 minutes per application and reclaims thousands of operational hours industry-wide.

In a recent development, fyndiq (Sweden): Swedish e-commerce marketplace Fyndiq (part of CDON Group) anchors its predictive analytics and data operations in Google BigQuery, dbt, and Google Cloud Storage. Fyndiq models transaction and product feed data to deliver near real-time business insights to merchandisers. Building sustainable AI businesses requires infrastructure that combines high computational performance with strict data governance and predictable cost efficiency. This week we introduced the Google for Startups Accelerator: Sovereign AI (Europe & Israel). This equity-free, 12-week hybrid program is tailored for late-Seed to Series A startups handling high-stakes, regulated workloads across sectors like GovTech, HealthTech, and financial services. Participating founders receive 1:1 architectural mentorship from Google Cloud engineers, technical advisory support to prepare for EU AI Act regulatory sandboxes, and hands-on guidance deploying across our tiered sovereign portfolio—from the Google Cloud Data Boundary and partner-operated clouds like S3NS to air-gapped Google Distributed Cloud environments and open-weight models like Gemma.

Recent findings suggest that amazon Connect Customer message templates, which personalize each message with details about its recipient, now support case fields from Cases and calculated attributes from Customer Profiles, such as a customer's most frequent contact channel. Companies that send updates about a claim, an order, or an application need each message to reflect that customer's record. Template authors can insert case fields, including custom fields that administrators define, and Connect Customer fills in the current value for each recipient every time it sends a message that uses the template.

According to recent reports, A claims manager at an insurance manufacturer can build one email template that pulls each claim's reference number and status from its case, so every policyholder receives an enhancement about their own claim. A retailer can add a custom calculated attribute, such as each customer's total orders in the past year, to a loyalty email so every customer sees their own count. Developers can pass these values when they render a template with the RenderMessageTemplate API.

You can use case and calculated attributes in message templates in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Africa (Cape Town), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Canada (Central), Europe (Frankfurt), and Europe (London).

To learn more, see Add personalized content to message templates in the Amazon Connect Customer Administrator Guide.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow.
  • This post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience.
  • Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow. In Part 1 of this series, you will learn how to systematically analyze inference performance and identify where the time is spent.

This post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience. The walkthrough uses AWS Trainium, a purpose-built AI chip for deep learning training and inference workloads, and TorchNeuron, its open source native PyTorch backend. TorchNeuron supports standard PyTorch workflows on Trainium, including eager execution, torch.compile, and standard PyTorch APIs, with minimal code changes. Additionally, TorchNeuron integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) to enable custom operators and performance optimization for Trainium hardware. By the end, you should know:.

Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.

Industry observers note that the Neuron backend uses PyTorch's PrivateUse1 extension point. This mechanism lets an accelerator integrate with the framework without adding a dedicated dispatch key such as cuda. The torch_neuronx package works with upstream PyTorch to register Neuron as a native backend for PyTorch code. For details about this extension mechanism, see Facilitating Latest Backend Integration by PrivateUse1.

You use two objects to profile a Neuron workload:.

The modes parameter selects the data streams to capture, such as device instructions and runtime traces. The capture_enabled_for_nc parameter selects the NeuronCores to trace. Setting correlate_device_time=True propagates device time from the trace into the key_averages() table, where you can compare CPU and Neuron device time. For the complete parameter reference and available ProfileMode values, see the NeuronConfig Profile Modes documentation.

Industry observers note that neuron Explorer is a browser-based viewer for the system trace, device timeline, and per-engine breakdown. You can access it through an SSH tunnel or the Visual Studio Code extension. In this post, you use Explorer to confirm what key_averages() reports numerically and inspect what happens between dispatches.

After profiling, the output directory contains the system trace and, when you capture device data, matched .neff and .ntff files. The Neuron Executable File Format (NEFF) contains the compiled Neuron executable, while the matching NTFF contains its hardware instruction trace. The files share a numeric hash that identifies them as a pair. To open the profile in Neuron Explorer, upload the complete output directory for a system or combined profile. For a device-only profile, upload the matching .neff and .ntff files individually. See Step 5: Upload your profile for the UI and command-line instructions.

For this first analysis, you profile RMSNorm, a small operation with a clear sequence of arithmetic and reduction operations.

You profile three implementations of the same operation:.

The scripts use the same inputs, profiler configuration, and schedule so the results are directly comparable.

All scripts to reproduce this work are available in the torch-neuronx examples directory.

It has been revealed that start by writing RMSNorm with individual PyTorch operations. Each line maps to one or more ATen operations and can create intermediate tensors.

Call the profiler with two arguments required for the Neuron backend:.

It has been revealed that the schedule uses wait=2, warmup=1, and active=1 across four prof.step() calls. This records one warm iteration without including initial setup overhead.

According to recent reports, call torch.neuron.synchronize() inside the profiler loop. Without this synchronization, the profiler can export before the device finishes and leave the Neuron time column empty.

Recent findings suggest that after profiling finishes, inspect the key_averages() table. Sort by self_privateuse1_time_total to place the operations with the highest device cost first. The table shown here is filtered to the RMSNorm operations that report Neuron device time. The full key_averages() output also includes CPU-side events such as allocations and host-to-device transfers.

The key averages table reveals that three aten::mul calls account for the largest share of Neuron device time.

Sources indicate that the table highlights which ATen operations ran, how often they ran, and how much time they spent on the CPU and Neuron device. aten::mul has the highest total device time because the function performs three multiplications.

It has been revealed that each row maps directly to the function. aten::mul runs for x * x, x * rms, and the final multiplication by weight. aten::mean reduces the last dimension. aten::add adds the epsilon value and triggers a host-to-device copy because the scalar starts on the CPU. aten::rsqrt computes the reciprocal square root.

Neuron Explorer follows an aten::mul operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to execution on the Neuron hardware lanes.

In Explorer, time flows from left to right and the event lifecycle flows from top to bottom. Each ATen operation follows the same pattern: creation in the framework lane, scheduling in the runtime lane as nrta_execute_schedule, and device execution in the hardware lane as nc_exec_running.

It has been revealed that the system trace view organizes events into lanes. In the Default grouping mode, labels follow the pattern instance/PID/subsystem/identifier:.

In eager mode, each operation runs independently. Use the dependency chain viewer to follow aten::mul.Tensor from the framework layer through runtime scheduling to device execution.

The dependency chain viewer highlights the lifecycle of one operation across the framework, runtime, and hardware lanes.

Industry observers note that replace the individual operations with PyTorch's built-in rms_norm function. Neuron lowers the operation to one fused kernel:.

The fused RMSNorm appears as one device operation in the key averages table.

The fused RMSNorm follows one framework-to-hardware path instead of dispatching each arithmetic operation separately.

Sources indicate that in the naive implementation, each operation crosses the dispatch boundary independently and follows its own framework-to-runtime-to-hardware path. In the fused implementation, one Python call covers the complete computation. The trace contains one dispatch and one hardware event, with no gaps between component operations.

For the final example, compile the original naive RMSNorm function with torch.compile.

In a recent development, with @torch.compile(backend="neuron"), TorchDynamo captures the Python bytecode as an FX graph and AOTAutograd lowers it to ATen operations. The Neuron backend receives the complete graph instead of dispatching each operation separately. It fuses the operations, optimizes memory access, and compiles the graph into a single NEFF artifact. The artifact runs as one hardware dispatch.

The compiled function appears as one Torch-Compiled Region in the key averages table.

The compiled graph follows one path through runtime scheduling and hardware execution.

In a recent development, the table highlights one device execution, as in Profile 2, but the code takes a different path. Instead of calling a purpose-built fused operation, the compiler discovers the fusion from the original Python function. In this run, the Neuron time is comparable to torch.rms_norm, at 375 μs compared with 403 μs.

Both torch.rms_norm and torch.compile fuse RMSNorm into one kernel dispatch. In these runs, either approach takes about one-sixth of the naive implementation's device time. Fusion removes the gaps between hardware executions and avoids materializing intermediate values such as x_sq and mean_sq between separately dispatched operations.

key_averages() demonstrates which operations consume device time, while its full output also reveals CPU-side setup and transfers. Explorer provides the corresponding visual trace. You can follow one operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to hardware execution and see the gaps that fusion removes.

You can use the same workflow on larger models: find a hotspot in the table, verify it in the trace, and then determine whether a fused operation or torch.compile can reduce its cost.

It has been revealed that in Part 2, we will move into the device-level profile. You open the NEFF, inspect the TensorEngine, VectorEngine, and direct memory access (DMA) breakdown, and place the kernel on the roofline to determine whether it is compute-bound or memory-bound.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that amazon Kinesis Data Streams now supports queues, a simpler and more cost-effective way to process a stream.
  • Queues in Kinesis Data Streams are powered by Amazon SQS.
  • Recent findings suggest that use queues for applications that process each record independently, such as log processing, order fulfillment, and notifications.

Industry observers note that amazon Kinesis Data Streams now supports queues, a simpler and more cost-effective way to process a stream. Because queues track the delivery state of each record, your consumer instances receive records instead of leasing shards, acknowledge each record when processing is complete, and scale beyond the number of shards. Kinesis Data Streams consumers can reduce the cost of processing data by up to 43% by using queues instead of the Kinesis Client Library. You no longer run a DynamoDB table or custom metrics, and you use compute more efficiently.

Queues in Kinesis Data Streams are powered by Amazon SQS. Built on that foundation, a queue delivers records at least once, redelivers records your consumers do not acknowledge, and provides built-in dead-letter handling for records that keep failing. Each queue publishes its own CloudWatch metrics, so you can scale consumer instances on records waiting to be received and alarm on records that repeatedly fail.

Recent findings suggest that use queues for applications that process each record independently, such as log processing, order fulfillment, and notifications. Use a stream consumer when processing one record depends on the records before it, such as live analytics, personalization, and anomaly detection. You ingest data once and let each application consume records through a queue or directly from the stream, with no change to your producers or existing stream consumers. For point-to-point messaging between application components, start with Amazon SQS. Choose queues in Kinesis Data Streams when the same records are needed by multiple applications.

It has been revealed that queues are available for data streams in On-demand capacity mode. For regional availability, see Supported AWS Regions. To get started, see the developer guide, install the Kinesis Data Streams skill from the Agent Toolkit for AWS, read the launch blog, and see the pricing page.

This report describes the design principles and systems engineering behind the series, spanning architecture selection, large-scale pretraining, and reasoning and agentic post-training. We study how sparse activation, attention design, model depth and width, and speculative decoding balance model capacity with computation, memory access, and execution overhead. Our pretraining infrastructure builds on MindSpore HyperParallel, combining topology-aware hybrid sharding, efficient distributed optimizer execution, and coordinated management of long-sequence workloads and activation memory. CPU affinity and core isolation further reduce host scheduling interference. Together, these mechanisms support the pretraining of a 285B-parameter model on 8,192 Ascend 910C cards, providing a concrete setting for the architectural and systems studies. For post-training, we introduce TeleGym, a unified agent execution platform that connects execution, evaluation, and trajectory construction to policy optimization. Disaggregated asynchronous execution, bounded oversampling, and partial rollout accommodate heterogeneous task durations while preserving trajectory continuity across policy updates. Together, these advances establish an Ascend-oriented training foundation for the continued development of Xing 4 across model scales and increasingly demanding reasoning and agent workloads.

#7649. Industry News: How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications

Industry News: How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2209 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.
  • In an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens.
  • The tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.

In an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens. This article previews some results from the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon: how we specialized the vocabulary around the cost of each token rather than its frequency, and cut measured inference cost by 77% without changing the base model.

The tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone. For a model specialized in a single domain, it can be one of the largest cost levers, and it is set before any training step.

It has been revealed that one of the systems we run in production is an automated grader for Portuguese essays, built on Qwen3-4B. It receives the essay, the prompt and the supporting texts, and returns a JSON assessment with a grade and a comment for each competency.

The model was already small, at 4 billion parameters, and had already been trained for the task. Its tokenizer, however, was still the original Qwen3-4B one, built for many languages and many kinds of text. In the grader, it was used for a single language, Portuguese, and a single response format. That had two costs: the text the grader writes on every request took more tokens than it needed, and at every generated token the model scored a vocabulary of 151,669 entries, including many this task almost never uses.

Sources indicate that we rebuilt that vocabulary with a method we call VocabX, keeping the same base model, the same data and the same training recipe. The numbers in this article come from the current version of the paper, still under review, and may change before publication.

According to recent reports, the leading language models read and write in tokens, and the tokenizer decides how text becomes tokens. The tokenizers of the leading general-purpose models are trained on large collections of text from many domains and languages, from source code to contracts to Chinese. For a general-purpose model, that choice makes sense.

For a model used in a single domain, it creates two kinds of waste at once.

In a recent development, the first is fragmentation. The tokenizer splits into many pieces exactly what the domain repeats most. In the grader, every response starts with the same JSON envelope, the same competency names, the same evaluation phrases. In contracts, it is the boilerplate clauses. In code, the identifiers. Each of these sequences costs several tokens where one would do, and the model pays for every one of them on every request.

The second is excess. The vocabulary carries tens of thousands of entries the domain never uses, and the model computes a score for all of them at every token it generates. A model tuned to grade American school biology exams will almost never write in Chinese, yet it computes the probability of every Chinese-language token at every step. The vocabulary splits into many pieces what the domain repeats most, and carries entries the domain never uses.

The natural reaction is to count tokens and try to reduce the count. But the count is not the bill.

Sources indicate that to see why a generated token costs more, it helps to look at how inference works. It has two phases. In prefill, the model processes the whole input in a single pass through the network: each weight read from GPU memory is reused for every input token, and the limit is compute. In decode, the model generates the response one token at a time, and each token needs a full pass. Each weight read is used only a few times, and the GPU spends most of its time waiting for data to arrive from memory: the limit becomes memory bandwidth.

This effect is strongest exactly where we operate: small models served with moderate batches. Batching requests splits the weight reads across them and eases the problem, but does not solve it. At every decode step, the model also reads the KV cache, the attention memory that holds the context already processed and grows with it. In the case we measured, the grader, a generated token costs 7.4 times a token read, but the ratio varies with the hardware, the problem, the batch size, the context length and other factors, and it can be larger than that. In general, the direction holds: generating costs more than reading.

Think of a shipping company that charges per box, but charges seven times more for outgoing boxes than for incoming ones. Reducing the total number of boxes helps. Reducing the outgoing boxes helps seven times more. A method that compresses input and output equally misses most of the possible savings.

The third component of the bill is the vocabulary itself. The model's last layer, the LM head, turns the internal state into a score for every possible token. To do that, it holds one row of parameters per vocabulary entry. In a model the size of Qwen3-4B, that matrix accounts for almost 10% of the parameters. It is a share that large models absorb without noticing, but it weighs on a small model.

Industry observers note that and the cost is not paid only once. The input layer looks up only the row of the token being read, but the LM head reads and multiplies the entire matrix for every generated token. Since decode is already memory-bound, every extra row is more data to move at every step. An entry the domain never uses costs exactly the same as a frequent one. That is why adding tokens can lower the count and raise the bill at the same time. VocabX does not include this term in its selection criterion, but it controls vocabulary size in two steps: the sub-word merge replaces the base vocabulary with a smaller, domain-specific one, and macros enter under a fixed budget. In the grader, the output layer went from about 152,000 to about 65,000 rows.

It has been revealed that adapting a model's vocabulary is not a new idea. Reference methods in the literature, such as fast vocabulary transfer (FVT), multi-word tokenization (MWT) and Liquid AI's in-place tokenizer expansion (in-place BPE), which continues BPE training from the original vocabulary, already reduce fragmentation. When we tested them on our problem, we found two limitations.

In a recent development, they choose tokens by frequency, not by cost. An expression that appears often in the input is worth more to them than one that appears less often in the response, even if the second is the more expensive one to serve.

They work on a single layer. They either adjust how words are cut into pieces, or merge whole phrases into one token. None of these three does both under the same criterion. And the grader's biggest waste was precisely in long, repeated spans such as the JSON envelope, which a sub-word method only reaches after merging each part, one by one.

VocabX addresses both limitations, plus a third problem that appears on the obvious path to solving the first.

In a recent development, first, we changed the question. Instead of asking how many tokens a candidate saves, we ask how much cost and time it saves. Each eliminated token is multiplied by the price of the field it appears in: system prompt, user message or model response. In the case we measured, the grader, a token saved in the response is worth 7.4 times one saved in the input, and the vocabulary is built accordingly.

Sources indicate that second, we work on both layers at once. Back to the shipping company: you can cut boxes by packing each item better, or by recognizing that the same twelve-item kit ships every week and sending the kit in a single box. VocabX does both. At the sub-word layer, it rebuilds how domain words are cut into pieces. At the multi-word layer, it looks for whole spans that repeat, from short expressions to full lines and JSON envelopes, and turns each into a single token, which we call a macro token. Both layers are chosen under the same cost criterion, each with its own budget.

According to recent reports, to find these spans, we use five miners, automatic searches for spans that repeat across the corpus, each specialized in one kind of repetition: long words, whole lines, expressions, complete sentences, and structures with punctuation such as JSON and tags. Averaged over eight corpora, the last one contributed the most, and on code it alone accounted for 17.5 points. Without all five, token reduction on the grader would drop by 55.6 points.

According to recent reports, third, we estimate what the sample cannot see. Choosing tokens by cost requires knowing how much each candidate still saves after the ones already chosen. Measuring that exactly would require reprocessing the entire corpus after every choice, tens of thousands of times. A common way to do this at scale is to measure on a sample of documents, and then a candidate absent from the sample gets zero gain.

An expression that appears 37 times in 50,000 documents reveals up in a 400-document sample only about 26% of the time. In a contracts corpus, only 16.6% of the candidates appear in a 400-document sample; the rest are never evaluated.

A candidate's gain has two parts. One is how much it saves over the entire corpus, and that can be counted exactly, without a sample. The other is how much of that saving is not yet covered by the tokens already chosen, and only that part needs to be estimated. For candidates the sample cannot see, we use a statistical estimate based on the behavior of the ones it can see, instead of zero. A candidate that is rare in the sample but frequent in the corpus is back in the running.

That change alone, with the same sample and the same budget, raised token reduction on a contracts corpus from 44.7% to 52.8%.

Sources indicate that to measure the real effect, we trained seven versions of the grader with the same base model, the same data, the same recipe and the same seed. The only difference between them is the tokenizer. All of them ran the same 500 requests on the same test machine, with an RTX 5090 GPU and the vLLM inference server, and cost was calculated from measured runtime.

Industry observers note that the model's response dropped from 350 to 101 tokens on average. Cost dropped 77.0%. Quality, measured by the bench score, which combines grading accuracy and the accuracy of screening off-topic or rule-breaking essays, rose from 0.703 to 0.810.

According to recent reports, getting there required a course correction. The first version of the vocabulary fused each competency's grade with the surrounding JSON into a single macro token. It was the most compact option, but quality dropped: its bench score was 0.689, below the production grader's 0.703. With the grade inside the macro, each combination of grade and structure became a different variant of the same token, and the model chose both in a single step. Giving the grade its own token cost 2 extra tokens per response, raised the bench score to 0.810 and, in the measurement, was even cheaper: a 77.0% reduction, against 73.3% for the fused version.

In a recent development, the lesson applies beyond the grader. Compression has a cost when the compressed span carries the very decision the model exists to make. The goal is not the cheapest possible vocabulary, but the cheapest one that preserves the tokens that matter.

To find out whether the gain was specific to our case, we compared VocabX with the three reference methods on five public domains (contracts, medical papers, scientific papers, news and Python code) and three model families (Qwen3, Llama-3.1 and Gemma-3). All methods used the same mining and test documents, and the same vocabulary ceiling.

VocabX compressed more than the strongest reference method in all fifteen combinations, by 1.2 to 9.3 points. In estimated inference cost, the pruned version of VocabX also led in all fifteen, with average margins of 10.2 points on Qwen3, 7.5 on Llama-3.1 and 13.6 on Gemma-3. On contracts, the pruned version reached 62.6% token reduction with 113,426 vocabulary entries, against 61.8% for the best in-place BPE configuration, which uses 207,803.

Recent findings suggest that vocabX does not make the model smarter. It makes the model stop paying for text it does not need to write piece by piece, and stop scoring a vocabulary it will never use. In our grader, that cut measured inference cost by 77%, with the same base model and the same training recipe.

Specialization usually starts with data and weights. It can also start one layer earlier, in the vocabulary.

The full method, the tables for every experiment and the discarded interventions will be in the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Product Manager, Cameyo by Google.

This IDC Market Note contains an analysis on how Cameyo by Google, a virtual app delivery (VAD) solution, helps organizations deliver any legacy application over the web.

Organizations are increasingly adopting generative and agentic AI as they look for ways to unlock more business value. Yet for many IT leaders, business-critical legacy desktop apps stand in the way—too essential to retire, too complex and costly to rewrite—yet unequipped for the security challenges and productivity opportunities of the AI era.

That doesn’t have to block your modernization strategy. By delivering Windows and legacy applications directly inside the Chrome browser, Cameyo by Google connects legacy workflows to Chrome Enterprise, ChromeOS, and Gemini—with zero replatforming required.

In a recent development, in a recent IDC Market Note, “Cameyo by Google: A Modern Bridge Technology Platform in Digital Workspace Transformation,” lead analyst Filippo Vanara examines how Cameyo reduces deployment complexity while enhancing security and lowering costs. Here are five of our key takeaways from the IDC Market Note:.

Enterprise modernization barriers make rewriting or replatforming legacy applications unfeasible for many organizations. The IDC report notes that "Cameyo is positioned as a strategic bridge between legacy application environments and modern, AI-driven digital workspaces." By connecting legacy systems to modern, AI-enhanced digital workspaces, Cameyo enables organizations to safeguard their existing technology investments.

Recent findings suggest that 2. Instant AI and security upgrades with Gemini and Chrome Enterprise.

Moving legacy apps into the browser immediately surrounds them with modern capabilities they were never built to support. RegimeCouncil: Paired-Evidence Routing For Memory Conflict Governance In LLM Agents

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (276 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.22113v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: Language agents rely on long-term memory to personalize responses across extended interactions, yet stored facts quietly go stale as the world changes, and an agent often learns that using memory hurt only through delayed feedback after acting on an outdated record. Before the memory store is updated, how far should that negative feedback propagate: should it suppress memory use only on future queries for that same fact (a local policy), or also across other stored facts (a global policy)? Existing memory systems implicitly fix one of these two sharing scopes at design time. We formulate this online scope choice under hidden validity and delayed feedback as memory conflict governance, and prove that neither fixed policy is sufficient on its own. We then propose RegimeCouncil, a lightweight paired-evidence router that retains both scopes as advisors and arbitrates between them online without retraining the LLM. Using revealed comparisons between answering with memory and answering without memory (the no-memory anchor), a Local Advisor tracks the latest outcome on the queried fact alone, while a Global Advisor pools recent outcomes across all stored facts. A Meta Governor follows the Local Advisor by default to avoid cross-fact interference and switches to the Global Advisor only when global pooling accumulates a strictly positive recent utility margin, guaranteeing finite-time switching under delayed feedback. Across LongMemEval enhancement streams and real-world historical drift on TempLAMA and TAQA with Qwen3-30B-A3B and GPT-4o, RegimeCouncil outperforms the better fixed-scope policy by 5.2-7.3 points on primary disagreement episodes and across all 30 held-out settings, while ablations show that removing any of its three modules reduces accuracy by 2-7 points.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Amazon Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall now automatically generates domain allow-lists from your VPCs' observed DNS query traffic, helping you enforce least-privilege DNS access and reduce the risk of DNS-based data exfiltration.

Previously, implementing a least-privilege model required security teams to manually analyze DNS query logs to identify the domains their VPCs depend on before deploying allow-list rules. This created operational overhead and delayed enforcement of a deny-by-default (walled-garden) posture.

It has been revealed that with automated allow-list generation, DNS Firewall analyzes DNS query traffic using a lookback window configurable from 1 hour to 7 days to create an allow-list of observed domains. It then continuously monitors DNS queries and flags newly observed domains, so you can review them before adding them to the allow-list. You can deploy the rule across multiple VPCs and accounts using AWS Firewall Manager or Route 53 Profiles.

It has been revealed that this capability is available at no additional cost to DNS Firewall Advanced customers, in all AWS Regions where Route 53 DNS Firewall is supported, except in AWS GovCloud (US) and Amazon Web Services China Regions. To get started, use the Route 53 DNS Firewall console, AWS CLI, or API.

To learn more, visit the Amazon Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall product page and the Route 53 DNS Firewall Developer Guide.

Latest Update: Testing artefacts are leaking data your compliance misses

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Automated testing helps protect software quality, but according to Napier AI, the reports, screenshots, logs and file exports it produces each day may be one of the least controlled data surfaces in many organisations.
  • Napier AI notes that test environments often hold real or realistic data, such as customer names, account numbers, contact details and financial figures.
  • The RegTech specialist argues that traditional redaction methods have not kept up.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Automated testing helps protect software quality, but according to Napier AI, the reports, screenshots, logs and file exports it produces each day may be one of the least controlled data surfaces in many organisations. As these artefacts move between teams, vendors and stakeholders, the sensitive information inside them can create serious privacy and compliance exposure.

Napier AI notes that test environments often hold real or realistic data, such as customer names, account numbers, contact details and financial figures. That data appears in the interfaces under test and is captured in the outputs. A report is attached to a ticket, a screenshot lands in a defect log, or a file export is sent to a vendor for troubleshooting. Each action seems routine, yet each one carries sensitive data further from the systems built to protect it.

The RegTech specialist argues that traditional redaction methods have not kept up. A decade ago, test suites ran on fixed schedules and produced a manageable number of outputs that a person could review before sharing. Today, continuous integration pipelines can trigger thousands of test runs a day. AI-assisted development is adding to this, as AI tools generate more code and test cases, often faster than governance frameworks can adapt.

Industry observers note that most existing redaction, Napier AI says, sits outside the workflow as an add-on. It might be a manual review, a plugin someone has to remember to switch on, or a post-processing step that gets dropped when deadlines tighten. These approaches also tend to focus on structured data fields, which leaves screenshots of live interfaces largely unprotected.

The financial risks are significant. GDPR penalties can reach €20m or 4% of global annual turnover, whichever is greater, and IBM’s Cost of a Data Breach Report 2026 puts the global average breach cost at $4.99m. Napier AI adds that the damage to customer trust may be even more costly.

For Napier AI, the core problem is structural: protection that relies on human vigilance is fragile by design. Its answer is compliance by design, built on three principles. First, redaction should happen inside the pipeline, at the moment an artefact is created. Second, coverage must include screenshots and file exports as well as reports. Third, every tool should pass security and compliance approval and hold recognised certifications such as SOC 2. Even then, sensitive data should be redacted before it reaches the tool.

The firm indicates this approach also improves productivity. Teams can share outputs without manual checks, audits move faster, and organisations can share artefacts with partners, auditors or regulators with more confidence.

It has been revealed that napier AI has applied these principles to its own practices. It developed its auto-redaction capability in house and built it into its automation testing and reporting across reports, screenshots and files. Every tool in that workflow passed security review before being allowed into its environment.

The company compares bolt-on compliance to a seatbelt that someone has to remember to fasten. Built-in protection, by contrast, works more like a car’s crumple zones, which function whether anyone thinks about them or not. Its central question for organisations is whether sensitive data is protected at the point of creation or only after it has already been exposed.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • We built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome.
